Fine-tuning involves further training the model on a smaller, domain-specific dataset with labeled examples, allowing the LLM to adapt to the new task. Fine-tuning can be primarily additive (i.e., new parameters are added to the transformer), reparameterized, or partial [74]. Full-model fine-tuning is computationally expensive and impractical for very large models, and could result in catastrophic forgetting. This is where Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods, such as LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) [75], come into play. LoRA works by injecting learnable low-rank matrices into the model’s layers, enabling the fine-tuning process to modify only a small subset of parameters, while the bulk of the pre-trained model remains frozen. The effectiveness of PEFT approaches, including LoRA, has been demonstrated in the broader context of machine learning, where fine-tuning efficiency is critical. Studies like Lialin et al. [76] and Fu et al. [77] demonstrate that PEFT approaches not only lower computational overhead but also prevent catastrophic forgetting, a common issue where the model loses pre-trained knowledge during fine- tuning. We refer the reader to [78] for a comprehensive review of continued pre-training and supervised fine-tuning domain adaptation strategies. 3) IN-CONTEXT LEARNING Instead of modifying the model’s parameters, LLMs can leverage the information provided in the context of the input (such as examples or instructions) to adapt to the task at hand. The auto-regressive nature of transformer models enables them to predict the next token based on the context, forming a deep understanding of the underlying data distribution. Auto-regressive inference can use the information provided in the prompt, assuming the prompt does not exceed the context length of the attention mechanism in the transformer. In-context learning can be achieved from zero-shot to few-shot learning, chain of thought (CoT) reasoning, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). In few-shot learning, the model is provided with a small set of examples or demonstrations within the input prompt, which helps it understand the task and generate the appropriate output. CoT reasoning is an inference strategy that breaks down complex tasks into intermediate steps, mimicking a human-like thinking process. Moreover, RAG further enhances in-context learning by allowing the model to access external databases in real time, improving the accuracy of generated outputs based on the provided context. This method is valuable because it offers flexibility. Therefore, the model can rapidly adapt to new tasks such as designing a novel circuit topology or modifying layout constraints based only on the examples it receives at runtime, without the need for retraining. LLMs have been applied to layout- level automation. For example, Layout CoPilot [26] simpli- fies human-tool interaction by converting natural language instructions into executable script commands. Similarly, GLayout automates layout generation through fine-tuning and RAG, eliminating the need to use GNNs on netlists [27]. Chen et al. investigate whether LLMs’ inherent knowledge and few-shot learning capabilities can enhance crucial aspects of BO in generating analog layout constraints [25]. Chang et al. propose LaMAGIC [29], a topology generation framework for power converter design. subsection V-C investigates the application in analog IC sizing. V. DISCUSSION: APPLICATIONS IN ANALOG IC SIZING Our review of past research highlights that ML models cannot solely address the analog sizing problem. Instead, ML should be viewed as an asset for data processing, helping to frame and guide optimization problems, as discussed in subsection III-B. Moreover, ML can be used to tackle the challenges outlined in subsection III-A through unsupervised learning methods, the representation learning of GNNs and generative models, and the ability of LLMs to learn linguistic and domain-specific knowledge. Data scarcity remains a challenge; however, online learning in RL frameworks, transfer learning, and fine-tunability of ML models have been studied as solutions to this problem. We summarize and cluster papers according to their optimization detail and learning objective in Table 1, and provide further references on approaches that utilize GNNs in Table 2. A. CANDID AUTOMATION METHODS One key challenge in applying ML to analog sizing is the scarcity and variability of training data. Real-world analog designs are often protected by intellectual prop- erty, and generating diverse labeled datasets is infeasible. Different learning paradigms supervised, semi-supervised, self-supervised, and reinforcement learning (RL) have been explored. RL agents learn by interacting with the design envi- ronment, and neural networks can enhance sample efficiency by constructing an online surrogate model of the environ- ment [88], or predicting the reward function [43]. RL has been increasingly applied to circuit sizing [90], [97], topology synthesis [98], and topology-aware sizing [95]. Transfer learning offers a promising path to reduce domain-specific training data requirements by leveraging knowledge from related tasks. However, RL presents challenges when applied to continuous and variable action spaces typical of circuit sizing and topology exploration, and defining a reward function that accurately reflects design goals is nontrivial. 1) TACKLING THE CURSE OF DIMENSIONALITY BO is the optimization engine behind much of the research on automatic sizing, but it suffers from cubic complexity. Similarly, the Cascaded Shallow Neural Net- work (C-SNN) model uses multiple shallow MLPs to size components iteratively, reflecting designer experience and bias while reducing training data requirements. Although currently aimed at generating initial sizes before layout verification, C-SNN can incorporate parasitic effects and constraints like inductance from EM simulations, making it a flexible tool for more comprehensive datasets [57]. Lastly, Shahane et al. [99] take a different approach using GNNs where each circuit is represented as a node in a graph, and leverage the closeness between node embeddings, along with a VAE, to create synthetic data. 3) RL-ENABLED AUTOMATION Learning to Design Circuits (L2DC) [100] represents an early application of RL to analog IC sizing, predating later advancements such as GCN-RL [97]. The RL framework uses observations derived from simulation tools such as Hspice and Cadence Spectre, including DC operating points, AC magnitude and phase responses, and transistor states. L2DC’s training charts show the agent first learns to meet hard-constraints (e.g., gain and bandwidth) and then learns to optimize good-to-have targets (e.g., area, power). Building on these foundations, more advanced methods have emerged. CRONus combines RL with neural simulators based on multiple MLPs to approximate reward functions to accelerate the design process [88]. TransNet enhances knowledge transfer across topologies by representing circuits as netlist-based matrices and utilizing MLPs to capture device and node interactions [83]. MACRO extends RL applications through multi-agent co-training, optimizing topology selection and sizing [95]. The Circuit Attention Network (CAN-RL) refines this approach with an actor-critic RL framework, incorporating stochastic layout-awareness to improve robustness against uncertainties and enable better knowledge transfer [101]. Other contributions, like DNN- Opt, address scalability challenges by introducing a sample- efficient two-stage optimization framework based on RL- inspired algorithms. This method integrates critical device identification to extend its applicability to industrial-scale circuits [52]. Finally, AutoCkt takes a layout-aware approach by combining RL with tools like the Berkeley Analog Generator, successfully validating its designs on advanced technologies such as 16-nm FinFET while accounting for process variations [84]. These advancements highlight the versatility and efficiency of RL-based methodologies in revolutionizing analog IC sizing. 4) PVT AWARE AUTOMATION Yang et al. reframe the sizing task as a constraint satis- faction problem with trust regions, focusing on efficiently meeting PVT-related constraints rather than achieving a global optimum [90]. By incorporating supervised learning to train model-based agents that mimic SPICE simulations, this method achieves stable convergence and rapid explo- ration of the design space. Its progressive PVT explo- ration strategy initially focuses on the most challenging PVT corner, verifying solutions across all corners while minimizing computational overhead. Validated in indus- trial applications using advanced TSMC 5nm and 6nm technologies, the method outperforms human designers by achieving superior area optimization and reducing design time. Vaz et al. take a different approach by utilizing artificial neural networks to approximate PVT corner performances. Their approach inputs circuit sizing and nominal performance data into a PVT regressor that estimates corner performances through multiple parallel neural networks [89]. Applied to a state-of-the-art Class C/D voltage-controlled oscillator, this method saves over 16 days of computational effort, balancing high accuracy with computational efficiency. The RoSE [86] Framework combines BO and RL to enhance convergence and sample efficiency in PVT-aware sizing. It uses BO to determine an optimal starting point for the RL agent and employs a variation-aware reward function incorporating sub-rewards for all PVT corners. Architecturally, it employs an MLP to process intermediate circuit specifications under PVT conditions and a GAT to capture device parameters. These features enable robust optimization and superior performance across multiple PVT corners. 5) HYBRID APPROACHES The integration of knowledge-based methods, such as the gm/ID approach, with advanced learning-based techniques offers a promising direction for analog circuit design automation. Experimental data demonstrate that when neural networks are trained on circuit data, the gm/ID metric is learned more effectively than traditional device sizing parameters [94]. The gm/ID methodology leverages a designer’s intuition to define feasible design spaces, making it highly effective for tasks like technology migration. Recent advancements utilize neural network surrogate models to predict performance parameters, enabling the application of automatic differentiation for optimization problems and achieving a fourfold improvement in training data sampling efficiency. However, its reliance on small-signal equivalent circuits limits its applicability to non-linear components, suggesting future work should explore novel RL frameworks and incorporate additional performance metrics like noise rejection. GNNs IN AUTOMATION GNNs have demonstrated significant potential in EDA by processing non-Euclidean data, which naturally represents circuit netlists as graphs. GNNs can perform representation learning on circuit structures, eliminating the need for manual feature extraction. GNNs can then apply ML techniques on the learned representations for node, edge, or graph level tasks [42]. This capability makes them well-suited for tasks such as topology exploration [23] and analog circuit labeling [62], [67]. GNNs have also been employed to model the relational data between circuit components and optimize layouts for parasitics [99], [102]. GCN-RL [97] was the first to use GCNs on graphs constructed from circuit netlists for op-amp sizing, demon- strating some transfer learning across technology nodes and similar topologies. However, the design is only verified at the schematic level and does not extend to unseen topologies. Li et al. provide an open-source framework to design and optimize a low-dropout voltage regulator using RL and a relational GNN in the SKY130 process [105]. Similarly, Hakhamaneshi et al. define another open-source framework, transferrable to unseen topologies, where a GNN trained on inexpensive DC simulation to predict node voltages can be fine-tuned to adapt to more complicated s such as gain of a circuit as a graph-level regression [59]. 1) PARASITIC AWARE AUTOMATION MLParest is an early work that incorporates parasitics into schematic-level sizing, reducing the number of iterations between pre-layout and post-layout design phases [91]. 58054 VOLUME 13, 2025

Hakhamaneshi et al. introduce their BagNet: Berkeley Analog Generator with Layout Optimizer to address the challenges of post-layout parasitics [10]. The method reduces the number of simula- tions required by evolutionary combinatorial optimizers by employing a DNN to filter out generated samples before subjecting them to time-consuming simulations. This DNN acts as an oracle, effectively predicting whether a design will meet the required specifications, thus drastically reducing the number of simulation iterations. BagNet integrates this discriminator into the optimization loop, learning from past designs to improve sample efficiency. Ren et al. propose a custom message passing function for their GNN, named ParaGraph, to predict layout-dependent parasitics [60]. Lastly, Liu et al. avoid layout generation by predicting parasitics using GNNs and BO [63]. 2) TOPOLOGY AWARE AUTOMATION Poddar et al. achieve joint topology optimization using a VAE to build an adaptive dataset of 360 op-amp topologies, as detailed in [22]. However, this approach is not easily extensible to various circuit blocks. CktGNN [106] encodes circuit graphs using a two-level GNN framework (nested GNN). CktGNN represents circuits as combinations of subgraphs in a known subgraph basis. It additionally intro- duces Open Circuit Benchmark (OCB) as an open-sourced dataset to assess and reproduce the results. Yang et al. have contributed many ideas to topology-aware optimization and dimensionality reduction of the design space using VAEs [23], [48], [104], [107]. Moreover, Yang et al. study the complexity of analog design space exploration and exploitation, and suggest dimension decoupling, dimension embedding, region restriction and region decomposition, and introduce Analog Circuit Optimization Benchmarks (ACOB) [103]. Yang et al. combine all the previous work into a unified framework to generate Op-Amps from specification to layout [24]. Refer to Table 2 for a summary of the methods. C. LLMs IN AUTOMATION LLMs represent a sub-domain of generative models, yet their application in analog design remains relatively unexplored. Practitioners should be aware of certain limitations when applying LLMs to this field: LLMs struggle with precise mathematical calculations, often requiring instructions to generate code that can verify or test their outputs. Addition- ally, they are prone to ‘‘hallucination,’’ meaning they may confidently provide incorrect answers if they lack specific knowledge. Despite these challenges, recent research has shown potential in adapting LLMs to analog IC design by employing prompt engineering and selective fine-tuning. In- context learning can be viewed as implicit fine-tuning since it produces meta-gradients through forward computation similar to explicit fine-tuning [108]. This work is the first to integrate large language models into standard cell layout design optimization, leveraging prompt engineering and an iterative ReAct framework to generate high-quality cluster constraints; the proposed methodology not only reduces cell area by up to 19.4% on industrial 2nm benchmarks but also ensures fully routable designs, addressing critical challenges in both performance-power-area optimization and routability. Nonetheless, the following subsections focus on the use of LLMs in circuit sizing. AnalogCoder: Lai et al. present a training-free, open- source LLM agent that automates analog circuit design through PySpice code generation, achieving rapid initial design with prompt engineering and a feedback-enhanced workflow [28]. AnalogCoder automates schematic-level tasks, yet the absence of topology-aware design and post- layout parasitic management limits its capability to accu- rately predict or mitigate parasitic or PVT variations. Experi- mental results show that AnalogCoder successfully generates 20 out of 24 targeted circuits, surpassing the performance of models like GPT-4o, yet it fails in high-complexity designs such as op-amp integrators and voltage-controlled oscillators. LADAC, however, utilizes few-shot learning and iterative prompt engineering to assist in parasitic-aware sizing for improved layout robustness [31]. ADO-LLM addresses complex circuit sizing by integrating BO with LLM in-context learning, making it well-suited for layout and parasitic-aware circuit sizing [30]. The model can infer design principles from a few example circuit layouts and their associated performance metrics. Provided with initial examples, ADO-LLM refines future designs based on perfor- mance metrics, achieving efficient, accurate multi-objective optimization without extensive retraining. SPICEPilot [109] is a prompt-steering approach to creating PySpice code based on user specifications using various commercially available LLMs. The paper introduces AmpAgent [110], an LLM-based multi-agent system for efficiently designing multi-stage amplifiers by automating literature analysis, mathematical reasoning, and device sizing. AmpAgent demonstrates significant improvements in design efficiency, iteration reduction, execution time, and circuit performance compared to traditional methods, showcasing the potential of LLMs in complex analog circuit design and performance porting. Future studies of joint topology exploration and sizing such as [98] could incorporate RL, VAEs, and symbolic modeling to jointly explore topology selection and circuit sizing. The success of circuit sizing automation, therefore, depends on the development of state-of-the-art topology exploration and layout generation tools. D. CREATE OPEN-SOURCE DATASET AND TESTBENCHES Establishing standardized datasets and test-benches, similar to other ML fields, would greatly accelerate research. While efforts like those by AICircuit [111], ACOB [103], and AnalogCoder [28] help create a diverse dataset of simple and complex analog circuit blocks, they only include schematic-level simulations and thus lack reliability against parasitics and PVT variations. Furthermore, generative models such as auto-encoders can be used to compress high-dimensional design spaces, facilitating efficient explo- ration without requiring labeled data, or generating synthetic training data. Research could explore how unsupervised methods like these can be better applied to analog circuit optimization. G. EXPERIMENT WITH NOVEL MULTI-AGENT RL (MARL) Research has shown that analog design cannot be solved in a zero-shot manner; instead, automation should mimic the approach of an expert engineer. MARL has been used to explore design space, balance between inexpensive and expensive simulations, and learn policies that avoid unreliable designs [49], [96]. Wen et al. achieve co-operative learning between agents by using a multi-agent transformer (MAT) to treat a team of agents as a sequence model [115]. MAT is trainable online and demonstrates high data effi- ciency. Novel approaches in MARL, such as MAT, enable the parallelization of multi-fidelity problems, as outlined in subsubsection III-B4. H. MULTI-MODAL AI Combining multiple data sources (e.g., netlists of open source circuits, research papers and textbooks) can help address data scarcity in analog design. Leveraging multi-modal AI can enhance models’ ability to integrate diverse information sources and improve overall performance. VII. CONCLUSION Our review summarizes the wide range of research that has contributed to practical AI-driven analog IC sizing. We provide a structured overview of references for various sizing methodologies, and highlight the contributions of MLPs, VAEs, GNNs, and LLMs to analog IC sizing using illustrative examples. Moreover, we review methods that address data scarcity, PVT variations, and layout parasitics, and we suggest future research directions. REFERENCES [1] B. text: ABSTRACT OF THE DISSERTATION Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach by Zhuofu Tao Doctor of Philosophy in Electrical and Computer Engineering University of California, Los Angeles, 2025 Professor Lei He, Chair Analog/mixed-signal (AMS) circuits traditionally require manual design efforts by experi- enced engineers. This process is labor-intensive, expensive, and often lacks explainability. Recently, researchers have employed large language models (LLMs) in various fields, showing potential for automating AMS circuit design as well. However, while state-of-the-art LLMs possess significant knowledge, they are incapable of managing the entire design process alone. To address this challenge, we present a series of data-driven methods to enhance AMS circuit understanding and design automation. We begin by addressing the multimodal LLM challenge of understanding schematics and parsing circuit topology. This limitation currently hampers the use of abundant schematics available in academic literature. We propose a schematic parsing algorithm based on ad- vanced computer vision techniques to convert schematics directly into netlists. Initially, we train an object detection model based on YOLO to identify individual schematic elements. Subsequently, we employ an instance segmentation model based on U-net to detect wires and collect connectivity between elements to generate netlists. By processing 2,686 schematics ii

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: from literature with this data transformation pipeline, we create the AMSnet dataset. To enrich its data modality, we manually annotate the schematics with functional traits and reconstruct them in OpenAccess format, making them usable in popular EDA software. With the data support from AMSnet, we are ready to automate circuit design. We introduce AMSgen, an LLM-driven design flow that spans from performance specifications to post-layout simulation. This process begins with a series of LLM inquiries to derive a block-level design strategy, which we convert into a list of relation-label pairs. Using these pairs, we query our dataset to retrieve subcircuit blocks and assemble them into a complete circuit topology. Next, we utilize Bayesian optimization (BO) to determine circuit sizing. This algorithm intelligently selects sets of parameters and performs simulations to ascertain the corresponding performance. Through a series of trials and errors, the algorithm eventually converges on an optimal set of parameters that achieve desired performance. If performance goals remain unmet after a maximum number of trials, we revisit the topology generation step, using the actual performance as a reference to suggest alternative circuit topologies through LLM knowledge. Our method is evaluated in two case studies, where we successfully generate an operational amplifier and a comparator without human intervention. Additionally, with support from analog cells (Acell), we introduce an automated layout step within the sizing loop, ensuring that the generated circuits consider physical design aspects such as parasitic effects, thereby enhancing reliability. A limitation of AMSgen is its reliance on BO for end-to-end simulation, which can be costly for larger circuits with more sizing parameters, as the search space grows exponentially. To extend our automated design process to larger circuits, we leverage analytical equations and propose a hierarchical design flow. Inspired by traditional engineering approaches, we first derive performance requirements for the subcircuits from the overall specifications, then optimize them independently. This significantly reduces the number of parameters we need to optimize in each loop, making the design approach more feasible. The entire process is driven by a dependency graph, ensuring that all theoretical calculations and subcircuit iii

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: optimizations are conducted in order, populating each parameter before it is required. This approach is evaluated on a SAR ADC (successive approximation register analog-to-digital converter) design, enabling the production of ADCs with 12-14 bits of resolution and up to 1MHz of sampling frequency, again without human intervention. In summary, we propose a series of methods to collect, transform, and utilize AMS circuit data in automated AMS circuit design. Our approaches allow us to design complex circuits such as SAR ADCs, comprising over 200 devices, with minimal human effort beyond the data collection step. For future work, our methods could extend to additional features such as testbench generation and further automation in data annotation to reduce human effort significantly. iv

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: CHAPTER 1 Introduction 1.1 Background Analog/mixed-signal (AMS) circuit design remains one of the most intricate and labor- intensive areas of electronic system development. Unlike digital design, which benefits from a high degree of automation and modular abstraction, AMS design continues to rely heavily on human expertise, domain-specific heuristics, and trial-and-error tuning. Crafting even relatively simple AMS blocks requires a deep understanding of both device-level physics and system-level specifications, along with an ability to navigate the subtleties of real-world parasitics, process variations, and layout constraints. Much of the design knowledge is tacit—passed down through experience rather than textbooks—and the iterative process of refining a circuit often hinges on intuition developed through years of hands-on work in lab and simulation environments. The difficulty in formalizing this knowledge has made AMS design automation a long- standing research challenge. Many steps in the process are not easily captured by determin- istic rules or symbolic reasoning. This lack of explainability, combined with the non-convex and environment-dependent nature of AMS design spaces, means that traditional algorithmic approaches struggle to replicate the decisions made by expert designers. While electronic de- sign automation (EDA) tools have advanced in certain aspects of verification and layout, true automation of the design phase—especially for analog and mixed-signal circuits—remains largely unrealized. 1

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: Recently, the emergence of large language models (LLMs) has reignited interest in au- tomating complex, expert-driven workflows. LLMs have demonstrated remarkable general- ization across diverse tasks, with some even exhibiting behavior akin to human reasoning and problem-solving. Their ability to encode and retrieve vast amounts of knowledge opens the door to a new paradigm of design automation—one that could potentially bridge the gap between rigorous theoretical analysis and the nuanced, experiential knowledge used by human designers. In principle, LLMs could learn to emulate expert behaviors, respond to design constraints, and adapt to iterative feedback in ways that go beyond conventional rule-based systems. However, when applied to AMS circuit understanding and generation, current LLMs show significant limitations. They struggle with tasks such as interpreting schematics, generating syntactically and electrically correct netlists, and producing reasonable component sizing. These frequent errors suggest that state-of-the-art LLMs lack sufficient domain knowledge in AMS electronics. Given that LLMs are fundamentally data-driven models, their performance can be greatly improved by curating and supplying high-quality domain-specific data. This motivates a new research direction: developing data-centric pipelines that enhance LLM capabilities in AMS circuit analysis and design, thereby moving closer to the long-standing vision of robust and reliable AMS design automation. 1.2 Approach To support large language models (LLMs) with the domain-specific knowledge they cur- rently lack, we first propose a comprehensive dataset—AMSnet—presented in Chapter 2. AMSnet is designed to mirror the diverse modalities of information that analog/mixed-signal (AMS) engineers routinely engage with across the design process. These modalities include schematic diagrams, netlists, functional annotations, layout metadata, and performance met- rics, among others. By encompassing a broad spectrum of design representations, AMSnet 2

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: enables a more complete learning signal for both model training and retrieval-augmented reasoning. To construct AMSnet, we developed a cross-modality data transformation pipeline ca- pable of converting human-readable schematics into machine-interpretable netlists. This pipeline leverages computer vision techniques to detect symbols, terminals, and wires within schematic diagrams, reconstruct their topological relationships, and generate accurate netlists in Cadence Spectre format. Additionally, to facilitate seamless integration with mainstream EDA tools, we created a utility to digitally rebuild schematics in environments such as Ca- dence Virtuoso. Recognizing that much of AMS expertise is implicit or experiential, we also manually annotated a subset of circuits with design rationales, functional descriptions, sym- metry constraints, and performance trade-offs. To ensure scalable and efficient data access, the entire dataset was encoded into a knowledge graph, where circuits and annotations serve as nodes, and design relationships and structural hierarchies define the edges. Building upon the data infrastructure provided by AMSnet, Chapter 3 explores an auto- mated design framework targeting small-scale AMS circuits, such as operational amplifiers and comparators. While state-of-the-art (multi-modal) LLMs are not yet capable of directly generating error-free AMS netlists, they do exhibit a promising ability to outline high-level design strategies and architectural block diagrams. We exploit this by tasking the LLM with generating abstract design blueprints, then performing knowledge graph retrieval-augmented generation (KG-RAG) to fetch and assemble relevant circuit fragments from AMSnet. Once a circuit topology is established, we apply Bayesian optimization to determine optimal de- vice sizing. Critically, our use of symmetry annotations from AMSnet allows for significant pruning of the search space, improving both speed and quality of convergence. Further- more, by leveraging abuttable analog cells (Acells), we automate layout generation and use post-layout simulation—rather than idealized pre-layout results—as the feedback loop for optimization, capturing parasitic effects and thus delivering far more realistic performance estimates. 3

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: Despite the success of this workflow in small-scale settings, practical limitations emerge when scaling to complex circuits. Bayesian optimization requires repeated interaction with computationally expensive simulators; while this is tractable for circuits with tens of param- eters, it becomes intractable for large-scale systems like analog-to-digital converters (ADCs), which may involve thousands of parameters and simulation runtimes of several hours. Chap- ter 4 addresses this challenge by introducing a hierarchical design flow. Instead of optimizing the full circuit holistically, we decompose it into smaller subcircuits. Using a library of analyt- ical performance equations, we approximate how global performance metrics decompose into local targets for subcircuits. A dependency-graph-based optimization scheduler then orches- trates subcircuit optimization in topological order—ensuring that any performance metric dependent on upstream components is computed only after its inputs are resolved. Using this approach, we successfully designed successive-approximation register (SAR) ADCs with varying specifications, reducing end-to-end design time to around an hour with zero human intervention after specification input—even though a single simulation of the full ADC can take over five hours. In summary, this dissertation demonstrates that data-driven approaches can play a piv- otal role in bridging the long-standing gap between formal engineering knowledge and the experiential intuition required for AMS circuit design. By systematically encoding expert be- haviors, structural patterns, and performance annotations into a rich, multi-modal dataset, and integrating this data into intelligent design workflows, we show that it is possible to extend the capabilities of modern machine learning models toward practical and reliable design automation. 4

text: CHAPTER 2 AMSnet: Schematic-Netlist Database 2.1 Introduction Large Language Models (LLMs) such as GPT-4 have been trained on vast corpora of tex- tual knowledge, demonstrating remarkable capabilities in various domains. These models have shown proficiency in providing reasonable explanations of how analog and mixed-signal circuits function. An illustrative example of this capability is presented below: User: I have two NMOS transistors which I want to connect into a current mir- ror, let the two transistors be M1 and M2, provide a list of required connections in this format: ”M1.drain - M2.gate” AI: Here is how you can connect them: M1.drain to M2.gate, M1.gate to M2.gate, and M1.source to M2.source. This configuration ensures that both transistors operate in the saturation region, essential for the current mirror to function properly. Figure 2.1: LLM correctly answers verbal AMS question As shown in Fig. 2.1, GPT-4 can accurately generate the correct connectivity required to configure a current mirror circuit. Despite their textual prowess, multimodal LLMs exhibit significant limitations when processing images. Particularly, these models struggle with reading and interpreting circuit schematics accurately. Consider the following interaction: 5

AI attempt 2: The schematic you provided contains five transistors. Figure 2.2: MLLM (GPT-4) fails to understand schematic. As depicted in Fig. 2.2, GPT-4 fails to accurately count the number of transistors within a given schematic, highlighting its limitations in visual data interpretation. A reasonable hypothesis is that the MLLM recognized the general shape of a 5-transistor operational amplifier (5T OPAMP), and simply responded with the number 5. The inability of multimodal LLMs to effectively interpret schematics could be attributed to the scarcity of training data. While there is an abundance of programming data available on platforms like GitHub, there is a notable deficiency in data for SPICE or other circuit netlist formats. Consequently, netlists generated by LLMs often cannot be used directly for 6

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: simulation or further development, unlike LLM-generated code, which is frequently ready for deployment. Additionally, existing training datasets are predominantly single-modal, lack- ing sufficient schematic representations adjacent to their corresponding netlists to facilitate effective training. In response to these challenges, we propose three initiatives: 1. A computer vision method specifically designed to convert schematics into netlists. 2. The application of this method to create AMSnet, a comprehensive database consisting of 2686 pairs of schematics and netlists derived from AMS literature. 3. An annotation format that encapsulates the functionality, strengths, and weaknesses of schematics to enrich the AMSnet database. The remainder of this chapter is organized as follows. Section 2.2 discusses the recent related works to parse schematics or produce similar databases. Section 2.3 delves into the schematic parsing algorithm. Section 2.4 describes the AMSnet database, including the annotation format and the arrangement of a knowledge graph for efficient retrieval. Section 2.5 discusses potential applications we can build upon AMSnet. 2.2 Related Work Prior to this work, there have been a number of similar AMS datasets. AICircuit [1] provides nine different types of AMS circuits with circuit schematics and a large number of simulation results for sizing. [2] contains five types of AMS circuits, including schematic images, netlists, and testbenches. ALIGN [3] provides a comprehensive collection of AMS circuits, along with well-sized parameters. AncstrGNN Benchmark [4] collects analog circuit netlists without schematic images. While these datasets have significantly contributed to the development of AMS circuit modeling and optimization, most of them are single-modality—primarily offering netlist data 7

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: without corresponding schematic diagrams or detailed annotations. While this suffices for traditional circuit simulation and optimization tasks, such datasets may not be well-suited for training modern multi-modal large language models (MLLMs), which are designed to process and reason over diverse data modalities, particularly images and text. For such models, it is essential to have aligned data tuples that capture the rich cross-modal relationships inherent in circuit design. Therefore, our work emphasizes the need to construct a dataset that not only includes netlists but also provides schematic images, functional annotations (e.g., circuit application, port roles, performance trade-offs), and other descriptive metadata to enable coherent and contextual understanding across modalities. 2.3 Schematic Parsing Algorithm The supervised learning approach for AI training utilizes multimodal data, which involves labeling one data modality with another that we aim to predict or understand. For instance, the renowned computer vision dataset, ImageNet, categorizes images with their respective classifications. This methodology not only laid the groundwork for numerous advancements in computer vision models but also highlights the potential of using similar strategies in other domains. Inspired by ImageNet’s success, we propose labeling schematics with corresponding netlists to create a rich dataset that future models can leverage for training. However, manually reading schematics and labeling netlists is a labor-intensive and costly task, often susceptible to errors. Furthermore, widely used netlist formats like SPICE (Sim- ulation Program with Integrated Circuit Emphasis) only capture the circuit topology, which is inherently non-unique. Modifications such as rearranging lines or renaming devices and nets can be done without altering the circuit’s functionality. Given these challenges, it is significantly more advantageous to employ an automated process for parsing schematics and generating corresponding netlists. Building upon these foundational insights, our proposed schematic parsing algorithm is 8

Initially, the algorithm focuses on element detection, where it identifies and classifies all symbols present in the schematics. These symbols encompass a wide range of schematic elements, including basic components like resistors and capacitors, devices such as transistors and amplifiers, and other critical symbols like VDD, ground, junctions, and ports. This step mimics the initial stage of human schematic reading, where one recognizes and categorizes the various elements visually before understanding how they are interconnected. Following this, the connectivity detection phase begins, which involves determining how these identified elements are interconnected within the schematic. This process is akin to tracing the wiring in a physical circuit, establishing a map of how signals flow from one element to another, thus completing the automated interpretation of the schematic layout into a structured netlist. Fig. 2.3 presents an overview of this algorithm. 2.3.1 Element Detection Object detection from images is a fundamental task in the field of computer vision (CV). Various models, such as YOLO (You Only Look Once) [5], have been developed to identify a wide range of objects in images, from inanimate objects like rocks to complex entities such as people. These models are not only versatile in recognizing everyday objects but are also 9

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: adept at detecting elements in schematics. They can categorize these elements based on their types and orientations, which is crucial for the subsequent connectivity detection step. In an ideal world, a dataset would already exist where schematic elements are meticu- lously labeled with precise bounding boxes and categories. Unfortunately, as AMSnet might be one of the first, if not the first, schematic-netlist datasets, there is a notable absence of such labeled data. This scarcity compels us to undertake the labeling process ourselves. However, manual labeling, as previously mentioned, is both labor-intensive and prone to errors. To overcome this challenge, we initiate the process by bootstrapping an initial dataset using template matching. We then progressively enrich this dataset through semi-supervised learning techniques, which allow for more efficient and accurate label generation as the model improves with incremental training. Template matching is a conventional algorithm that operates without machine learning. It involves matching a predefined template image to various regions within a source image using a sliding window approach, identifying areas that visually resemble the template. This method is particularly effective in fields like AMS where schematics are typically printed in a uniform style. Much like how every character or digit in a specific font appears identical, schematic elements are also consistently styled across various documents. This uniformity provides an ideal scenario for employing template matching, enabling efficient and accurate detection of these elements in schematic diagrams. Specifically, at each position of the sliding window, the algorithm calculates the similarity between the template and the feature. Whenever the similarity exceeds a certain threshold, the feature is considered a match. In our application, the template may be a manually cropped PMOS transistor in a specific orientation. The matched features would be all PMOS transistors in the same orientation across each schematic. Following [6], the normalized cross-correlation function is presented in Eq. 2.1. u, v are the top-left coordinates of the sliding window, x, y are the dimensions of the template, f(x, y) is a specific coordinate on the feature, t(x − u, y − v) is the matching coordinate on the template, fu,v is the mean of 10

text: the sliding window, t is the mean of the template, and γ(u, v) is the similarity between the template and the feature at the current window position. This method significantly reduces our hand-labeling effort from thousands of elements across the literature to tens of unique element types. γ(u, v) = P x,y[f(x, y) − fu,v][t(x − u, y − v) − t] { P x,y[f(x, y) − fu,v]2[t(x − u, y − v) − t]2}0.5 (2.1) Despite being more cost-effective than manual labeling, template matching is time- consuming compared to deep learning models because each template must be matched individually. In contrast, deep learning models like YOLO can identify all objects simul- taneously. For example, applying template matching to about 1000 schematics extracted from [7] using 50 templates takes over an hour, while YOLO requires about 12 minutes for training and only a few seconds for inference. Consequently, we adopt a semi-supervised approach where we initially train a model using data from template matching and then apply this model to label the remaining schematics. After each round of object detection inference, we manually inspect the results. If some elements are not detected, we mark them as new templates and repeat the process. This iterative method ensures that all elements are accurately labeled from the current literature before proceeding to the next, optimizing both accuracy and efficiency. At the end of this process, we manually evaluate the recall metric of the element detection results, and the overall recall was 97%. At this point, we have the location, orientation, and class labels for all elements in our schematics. 2.3.2 Connectivity Detection: Traditional Approach With all schematic elements identified, we can now focus on interpreting wires and pars- ing their connectivity. We propose two different methods for this purpose: a traditional method that utilizes search algorithms and a machine learning method that employs in- stance segmentation models. We will compare these methods in terms of their strengths and weaknesses. 11

text: The traditional method relies on two assumptions: 1) all nets are represented by solid lines on the schematic diagram, and 2) without a junction, two intersecting wires are not considered connected. While these assumptions may not always hold true, they apply to the majority of the schematics we have collected from literature and serve the purpose well. starting pixels starting element N1 Groups: [ {N1, M1}, {M1}, {M1, M2} ] M1 M2 (a) (b) (c) Figure 2.4: Grouping neighboring elements for net detection The first step involves identifying all immediate connections by breadth-first searching across wire (i.e., black) pixels. Starting from each pixel on each bounding box, the algorithm expands into neighboring wire pixels in all directions until it encounters other bounding boxes, collecting all visited bounding boxes along the way. This step groups elements into clusters, each representing a connection. Fig. 2.4 provides an example. Starting from the wire pixels on the bounding box for PMOS M1, three separate searches result in three groups: N1, M1, M1, and M1, M2. These correspond to the nets connected to the source, gate, and drain pins of M1, respectively. Naturally, we apply this to every element on the schematic. Each group of bounding boxes falls into one of four possible cases: 1) The group contains only the starting bounding box, as depicted by the green group in Fig. 2.4. In this scenario, no connectivity is detected. 2) The group contains exactly two bounding boxes, illustrated by the blue and brown groups in Fig. 2.4; here, the two bounding boxes are connected. 3) The group consists of an odd number of bounding boxes (more than two), which likely indicates that a junction has been omitted. However, the algorithm cannot determine which 12

text: subset of the group is actually connected and which is merely intersecting. Therefore, we flag the entire schematic as an exception; manual attention is required to correct it before further analysis can proceed. 2D convolution create intersection redo grouping Groups: [ {N1, N5}, {N2, N5}, {N3, N5}, {N4, N5} ] rerouting Groups: [ {N1, N3}, {N2, N4} ] N1 N2 N3 N4 N2 N1 N5 N4 N3 N1 N4 N5 N2 N3 Figure 2.5: Handling intersections for net detection For the last case, there is an even number (more than two) of bounding boxes in the group, as illustrated in Fig. 2.5. We assume that the schematic has not omitted any junctions; thus, the intersecting wires are not considered connected. To address this, we locate the intersections by applying a 2D convolution to the searched wiring. The area around an intersection typically contains a higher density of wire pixels, allowing us to identify the indices with the highest values as the intersection points, which we then add to our labeled bounding boxes. Subsequently, the algorithm resolves the four-box cluster by repeating the grouping process, connecting each of the four bounding boxes to the intersection. For groups with more than four bounding boxes, each iteration reduces the group size by two until each is left with just two bounding boxes. It is important to note that line weights and layout may influence this step, making the dimension of the convolution kernel a tunable parameter. In 13

text: this study, the convolution kernel dimension is set to the average size of the junction points previously identified during object detection. This is based on the assumption that wire intersections generally match the size of junctions, regardless of their connectivity status. Thus, as Fig. 2.5 demonstrates, intersection N5 is roughly the same size as junctions N1-4. Now that we have identified the intersection point, we order the connections to it by angle, similar to the method shown in Fig. 2.7 but applied to the intersection rather than elements. Given that there are always an even number of connections to each intersection (typically exactly four in practice), we assume that opposite wires are connected to each other. We thus split the list of connections into two halves and pair connections that hold the same position in their respective ”half lists.” For instance, in Fig. 2.5, the list of connections to intersection N5 sorted by angle could be [N1, N2, N3, N4]. This list would be split into [N1, N2] and [N3, N4], and we would connect N1 with N3, and N2 with N4 to effectively resolve the intersection at N5. (a) Overlaid markings (b) Partial highlighting 2.3.3 Connectivity Detection: Machine Learning Approach While the traditional method is effective for many schematics, it does not universally apply to every schematic available, and may fail when its underlying assumptions do not hold. A primary limitation of the traditional method is its reliance solely on observing wire pixels as they appear, without incorporating any contextual information such as the location of elements and their connections. Consequently, it might struggle to distinguish actual wires from other illustrative markings (e.g., the boxes in Fig. 2.8(a) could be misinterpreted as wires). To mitigate this, one might assume that such markings typically appear in different colors and employ techniques like binarization to filter them out during a preprocessing step. However, this approach could introduce new problems with different types of illustrations, as shown in Fig. 2.8(b), where parts of the schematic are depicted in a different color and might be unintentionally discarded. To address these special cases, we propose another method for connectivity detection that employs a deep-learning-based image instance segmentation model. This approach ac- curately determines whether lines represent wires and identifies which wires are connected to 16

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: each other, leveraging contextual information. Instead of hard-coding heuristics to determine connectivity, we rely on a training dataset to guide the decision-making process, and prove to effectively differentiate between wires and other illustrative markings. This approach is significantly more robust than relying on hard-coded heuristics. Previous research on wire segmentation and net detection often utilizes proposal-based instance segmentation methods, such as YOLO11-seg described in [8, 9]. These methods initially generate potential bounding box proposals, which are then refined through a dedi- cated segmentation module. However, they frequently struggle to fully encapsulate all pixels of a wire within a single proposal and may inadvertently include pixels from multiple nets, leading to suboptimal segmentation results. Additionally, the survey in [10] explores end- to-end instance segmentation techniques but reports difficulties in accurately distinguishing intersecting nets. oha encoder1 encoder2 encoder3 encoder4 decoder1 decoder2 decoder3 decoder4 attention attention attention cross handling connected components (b) split nets detect cross netk (a) 1 3 2 4 Figure 2.9: The proposed two-stage net detection method. (b) Detecting connected components, then perform split and merge operations at intersection points to identify the nets. 17

text: To overcome these challenges, we propose a more robust and efficient two-stage approach. This process begins with a semantic segmentation network, specifically U-net [11], to segment all wires and produce wire masks, as depicted in Fig. 2.9(a). These extracted wire masks are subsequently post-processed to accurately separate intersecting nets, as illustrated in Fig. 2.9(b). By eliminating the need for bounding box proposals, our method enhances segmentation accuracy and ensures precise delineation of individual nets, substantially im- proving the quality of the segmentation outcomes. Note that despite the noticeably inferior performance, YOLO11-seg would not require post-processing steps, therefore completely skips Fig. 2.9(b). While the previously mentioned methods are effective with clean schematics, they often struggle to segment nets accurately in noisy schematics. An example of this is illustrated in Fig. 2.8(a), where rectangles are drawn over the schematics. These noises, typically overlay markings used for illustrative purposes, can significantly interfere with the interpretation of schematics. Data augmentation is a widely used technique in machine learning to enhance the robust- ness of models by modifying raw training data. In this context, assuming the availability of sufficient training data and a reasonable distribution of data, the proposed model is de- signed to handle data noise inherently. Therefore, we augment the raw schematics with rectangles and text markings without altering the net mask labeling. We generate mocked markings randomly over the schematics, taking care to ensure that these rectangles do not overlap directly with the schematic elements. Following this augmentation step, the trained model is capable of successfully detecting wires through the mocked markings and effectively managing these challenging scenarios. After device and wire recognition, the flow needs to understand how they are connected to form nets. Given the segmented wire masks from the above steps, those that do not intersect each other belong to separate connected components. We assign a unique net label to each connected component. Fig. 2.9(b) shows an example of wire masks that interconnect and 18

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: are affected by cross lines. In this case, a mask is applied to the area around the intersection points, which splits the connected component at the intersection. Then, the tool merges the opposite connections to precisely identify the locations of multiple nets. Specifically, it orders all four connections to the intersection based on the angle between the connecting points and the center of the intersection, as shown in the green and purple numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 in Fig. 2.9(b). Finally, the connections 1, 3 and 2, 4 are grouped to resolve the intersection. At this point, we reproduce the connectivity detection functionality via machine-learning- based methods, and we no longer require context-unaware, hard-coded heuristics and as- sumptions. 2.3.4 Netlist Generation Results We train our models on a dataset split into training, validation, and testing subsets consisting of 1986, 500, and 200 schematics respectively. For element detection, we employ YOLO11, training it over 500 epochs with a batch size of 16, using the other default parameters of the model. For wire segmentation, we utilize two models: U-net and YOLO11-seg, and we compare their performance. The U-net model is trained for 1000 epochs with a batch size of 32, adhering to the default parameters set for this model. On the other hand, YOLO11- seg is trained for 1500 epochs with a batch size of 16, also using its default settings. All experiments are conducted on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. For the evaluation of netlist generation, we categorize three test sets into varying levels of difficulty—easy (80 schematics), medium (70 schematics), and hard (50 schematics)—based on the complexity of the circuit topology as well as the quality and style of the schematics. We manually assess the test set schematics using four metrics: high element count (10 or more elements), crossing wires, overlaid markings, and low resolution. Schematics that meet none of these criteria are classified as “easy”; those that meet exactly one criterion are labeled as “medium”; and those that meet two or more are designated as “hard”. Model Easy Medium Hard Unet [11] 90.19 84.17 80.39 YOLO11-seg [9] 83.62 71.10 73.11 Table 2.1: Netlist generation F1 scores The evaluation of these results is conducted using a confusion matrix. For each netlist component (excluding common elements such as VDD, GND, ports, etc.) and each net connection in the ground truth netlist, the following criteria are applied: • If a component or connection is correctly predicted in the predicted netlist, it is recorded as a true positive. • If a component or connection is missing from the predicted netlist or is predicted incorrectly, it is recorded as a false negative. • If a component or connection that does not exist in the ground truth is erroneously predicted (e.g., an extra capacitor or an unnecessary connection), it is recorded as a false positive. From these metrics, we calculate precision, recall, and subsequently the F1 score, which are reported in Table 2.1. Notably, incorrect type predictions, such as misidentifying a capac- itor as a resistor, are also classified as false negatives. This methodology ensures a thorough 21

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: and precise evaluation of the effectiveness of our wire detection and netlist generation algo- rithms. Given that different netlists can have varying element names and net names, direct com- parisons might not accurately reflect the effectiveness of the models. Therefore, we account for all possible permutations between ground truth names and predicted names to ensure a fair evaluation. For instance, consider netlist ckt 192 depicted in Fig. 2.10(a), where the predicted netlist might name elements as I0 and M9-12, and net names as VDD, VSS, and net2-6. If the ground truth labels VDD as “net1”, the correct permutation would match net1 with VDD, among other matches. To quantify this, we report the F1 score based on the best possible permutation that aligns the predicted names with the ground truth names. How- ever, as the complexity of computing permutations grows exponentially with the number of elements and nets, we sometimes manually determine the F1 score when the schematics are too complex. Furthermore, since we have the net positions through instance segmentation, we can compare them with the ground truth and secure a subset of net matches, significantly reducing the search space. 2.4 AMSnet Database With the schematic-parsing algorithm at our disposal, we are equipped to build a com- prehensive database by collecting and processing raw schematic images. Beyond just the fundamental content of schematics and netlists, we integrate several additional types of in- formation. The schematic parsing process highlights the crucial role of positional information for both elements and wires, which enables us to digitally reconstruct schematic images ac- curately. Although schematics alone offer limited utility for circuit design automation, their value can be greatly enhanced through functionality labeling. Section 2.4.1 provides an in-depth explanation of the detailed positional information we extract, utilize, and refine to construct digital schematics. Section 2.4.2 delves into the work 22

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: on functional annotation and discusses the knowledge graph structure we employ to organize and store data within AMSnet. 2.4.1 Digital Schematic Generation While generating netlists from circuit schematics enables programmatic use and supports downstream tasks, such as the automated parameter sizing method described in the next chapter. Having only the netlist is insufficient for practical adoption. Engineers are far more accustomed to working within EDA environments rather than manipulating raw netlists. Moreover, although our element and connectivity recognition performs reliably, occasional inaccuracies are inevitable. In such cases, visual inspection and manual correction through a schematic view is significantly more intuitive than examining a text-based netlist. To bridge this usability gap, we introduce a digital reconstruction workflow that recre- ates the original schematic in the OpenAccess format, compatible with widely-used EDA tools such as Cadence Virtuoso. This enables both manual verification and further design development by engineers in a familiar interface. Unlike netlist generation, which only requires topological information, schematic recon- struction demands spatial data—specifically, the positions and orientations of elements and the routing paths of interconnects. This process resembles a placement-and-routing step, aiming to preserve the visual structure of the original schematic as faithfully as possible. Our element recognition algorithm already provides the position and orientation of each component, so the main challenge lies in reconstructing the wiring. To achieve this, we define and extract a set of key points from the wire pixels. These key points fall into three categories: 1. End points: terminal points of wires that connect to components. 2. Diverge points: junctions where multiple wires intersect. 23

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: 3. Turn points: locations where wires change direction significantly. We first apply skeletonization to the wire pixels, reducing each interconnect to a one- pixel-wide structure. We then perform a depth-first search (DFS) to identify end and diverge points: a DFS step that terminates defines an end point, while one that splits into multiple traversal branches indicates a diverge point. A second DFS tracks directional continuity along the skeleton. Abrupt changes in direction exceeding a certain threshold are flagged as turn points if they are not already ends or diverges. Finally, we merge all neighboring points. These extracted key points effectively compress the wire data into a compact representa- tion suitable for reconstruction. The wires are then reassembled in OpenAccess by connecting the corresponding key points. To improve schematic readability and aesthetics, we apply a post-processing step that aligns adjacent key points. Horizontally or vertically neighboring points are snapped together to straighten wires and produce cleaner, parallel routing. Additionally, pin offsets from each element’s location are treated as key points and included in the alignment step to ensure proper visual and functional integration within the schematic. This reconstructed schematic not only supports usability within EDA software but also serves as a direct visual reference for comparison against the original input. Manual correc- tions can be applied efficiently, and we envision future enhancements where machine learning models assess the similarity between the original and reconstructed schematics. This could enable automatic alignment and correction, a direction we plan to explore in future work. 2.4.2 Functionality Annotation In addition to schematics and netlists, we also include annotations to enrich the circuit data. We define two types of annotations: local and global. Local annotations describe one or more elements within a circuit, while global annotations pertain to the entire architecture. 24

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: The purpose of local annotations is to guide the usage of the circuit. In this work, local annotations are hand-labeled. Examples include identifying nets as inputs, biases, outputs, or labeling groups of elements as building blocks, such as current mirrors or differential pairs. An important type of local annotation is the labeling of sizing constraints. These mark specific sets of elements to adhere to constraints such as symmetry in transistor lengths and widths. These constraints, typically derived from expert insights and design experience, play a crucial role in the sizing process by reducing search space and computation costs. Net labels, on the other hand, are used to connect the pins of circuits to each other and to testbenches. The purpose of global annotations is to guide topology selection, helping to choose one circuit over others. It is common for individual circuits not to have universally recognized names. Instead, they are often described by their elements or known for their specific functionalities. For example, an engineer might describe an op-amp by its stages or choose it for its exceptional performance in a particular area. To facilitate this information retrieval process, we label each circuit with architectural descriptions, such as performance specialties and subcomponents. We take advantage of the fact that the source literature, from which we initially obtain each schematic, likely includes some verbal descriptions within its context. We manually summarize this information into qualitative descriptions in the form of key- value pairs, such as gain: high or load: current mirror. We take a further step by producing JSON files to introduce more structure into our annotation data. Fig. 2.11(a) illustrates annotations on a circuit, while Fig. 2.11(b) presents the local and global annotation files for the given circuit. Since individual JSON files may share numerous labels, we simplify the data retrieval process and reduce data volume by merging equivalent annotations to form a knowledge graph. A knowledge graph (KG) is a structured form of knowledge representation that delin- eates the relationships between entities. In a KG, nodes typically represent entities, while edges denote various semantic relationships between these entities. The fundamental unit 25

There are several promising applications of the AMSnet dataset. In the following chap- ter, we will demonstrate how this database can significantly enhance AMS circuit design automation. Specifically, AMSnet aids in ensuring topological correctness—a critical step, as multimodal large language models (MLLMs) commonly make errors in generating ac- curate circuit topologies. Moreover, AMSnet provides an ideal environment for developing automated validation tools that verify topology correctness in LLM-generated netlists. Additionally, the rich annotations within AMSnet facilitate the generation of diverse question-answer pairs suitable for training MLLMs. These pairs cover essential skills in AMS circuit engineering, including circuit perception, analysis, and design reasoning. We intend to explore these training applications extensively in future research. Looking ahead, we plan to further expand AMSnet to better replicate the practical experiences of AMS engineers. Specifically, future iterations will incorporate detailed sim- ulation data beyond qualitative descriptions, capturing quantitative results, precise wave- forms, and interpretations of circuit performance. By incorporating common errors and their corresponding solutions, AMSnet will closely mimic the abundant coding forums currently available to software engineers, significantly elevating the state-of-the-art in AMS design automation. 28

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: CHAPTER 3 AMSgen: LLM-Driven Automated Circuit Generation 3.1 Introduction Digital circuit synthesis is extensively utilized in electronic design automation (EDA) [12], allowing contemporary large-scale digital integrated circuits (ICs) to advance in accordance with Moore’s law. However, the automation in analog and mixed-signal (AMS) circuit de- sign lags significantly behind that of digital design [13]. AMS circuits are primarily custom- designed today, heavily relying on human experts to determine circuit topologies and com- ponent sizing. This time-consuming and labor-intensive design process significantly hinders the scalability of AMS circuits. Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown potential to address various EDA challenges [14], offering new hope for automatic AMS circuit design. However, the availabil- ity of high-quality digital circuit data on the internet, such as Verilog code, far exceeds that of AMS circuits, mainly represented by netlists [15]. Consequently, LLMs have been exten- sively applied in the digital circuit domain, achieving significant advances in RTL code gener- ation [16, 17]. However, their application in AMS circuits remains exploratory. Researchers use LLMs to assist in analog circuit topology design and transistor sizing [15, 18, 19, 20]. Compared to traditional AI methods such as reinforcement learning (RL) and Bayesian op- timization (BO), LLMs offer greater flexibility in interaction, knowledge transfer, expansion capabilities, and interpretability of design solutions. Due to the scarcity of public AMS circuit netlist datasets, LLMs are insufficiently trained 29

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: to produce accurate netlists with correct topology and reasonable device sizing [18, 15]. Researchers have enhanced the performance of LLMs in designing AMS circuits by training them with datasets collected for specific circuits [18], or by employing prompt engineering techniques including chain of thought (CoT)[21], ReAct (Reason + Act)[22], and in-context learning (ICL)[23, 24, 15]. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is also used to supplement LLMs with additional knowledge without requiring expensive retraining[20]. Building upon the AMSnet dataset, we propose AMSgen, an automatic AMS circuit gen- eration framework. AMSgen aims to generate fully sized netlists from performance specifica- tions. Starting with high-level design strategies generated using LLM, AMSgen describes the circuit architecture using subcircuits. It autonomously retrieves matching subcircuits from AMSnet and assembles them into a complete topology via predefined block-level schematics. Guided by local annotations to reduce the search space, AMSgen automatically optimizes the transistor sizing through BO. If the generated design does not meet performance spec- ifications, AMSgen adds the current design and achieved performance to ICL as historical unsuccessful designs, and returns to the LLM-based strategy generation step. The process iteratively generates unique new designs until all performance goals are met. The remainder of this chapter is organized as follows. Section 3.2 discusses recent works related to generating AMS circuit topology, sizing, and layout. Section 3.3 describes the AMSgen workflow. Section 3.4 explores two case studies on OPAMP and comparator design. Section 3.5 discusses the overall contributions from AMSgen and potential future work. 3.2 Related Work 3.2.1 Machine Learning for AMS Circuit Design The automatic design of AMS circuits primarily includes topology synthesis and transistor sizing. In the era before LLMs, traditional machine learning or deep learning methods encode AMS circuits into strings [25], trees [26, 27], or graphs [28, 29, 30], and use methods 30

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: such as evolutionary algorithms, BO [31, 28], and reinforcement learning [29] for automatic topology design. CktGNN [30] proposes a two-level GNN framework that simultaneously automates circuit topology generation and device sizing. [31] It maps the block-level model of the circuit as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) and uses a variational graph autoencoder and BO for bi-layer optimization. LLMs demonstrate remarkable capabilities in numerous EDA tasks, such as Verilog and RTL code generation [32]. Recent efforts also explore using LLMs to directly generate ana- log circuit topology [18, 15, 33, 34]. However, due to the scarcity of AMS circuit topology data in pretrain datasets, these efforts are not very effective. Artisan [18] trains an LLM for the automatic block-level design of OPAMPs. However, the OPAMP-specific knowledge used to train their LLM cannot be smoothly generalized to other types of circuits, such as comparators and LDOs. AnalogCoder [15] does not retrain the model but uses carefully designed prompts to leverage the LLM’s capability to generate netlists. Due to the precise requirements of AMS circuits, multiple attempts and iterations are needed to achieve accu- rate results, if possible. LaMAGIC [33] achieves automated analog circuit design through supervised fine-tuning, automatically designing power converters consisting of three to six components. The transistor-level topological correctness of these methods relies on model knowledge, and may not be robust enough to scale to larger circuits. In this work, the correctness of the generated topology is guaranteed by the correctness of the dataset rather than relying on the LLM response, and is therefore more robust. 3.2.2 Sizing The goal of analog integrated circuit sizing is to determine the parameters of circuit compo- nents, such as transistors, within a given topology to meet design objectives. However, the substantial intra-class and inter-class variations, coupled with varying design goals across different circuit types, render the sizing process for analog integrated circuits particularly challenging. Researchers extensively study the automation of this process, primarily cate- 31

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: gorizing the methods into two types: 1) knowledge-based and 2) optimization-based. For knowledge-based methods such as [35], circuit designers create predefined schemes and equa- tions to calculate transistor sizes. However, deriving design schemes for every existing circuit topology is very time-consuming and also requires continuous maintenance to keep up with the latest process technologies. On the other hand, LADAC [20] designs the first LLM agent for analog circuit sizing based on ReAct [22]. By constructing an expert knowledge base, integrating ICL and CoT for decision-making, LADAC successfully derives transistor parameters for multiple circuit topologies and satisfies their respective design specifications. Optimization-based methods treat the performance of circuits as a black-box function and use heuristic algorithms [36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 41, 42] or surrogate model approaches for optimiza- tion [43, 44, 45, 46, 47]. The use of Gaussian processes as surrogate models in optimization methods is widely studied. ADO-LLM [19] combines an LLM with BO, using both the LLM and the acquisition function to determine the next sampling point. However, it does not discuss how to incorporate PDK technology nodes into their workflow, despite the fact that PDKs play an important role in the sizing process. Previous optimization-based methods include expert insights to reduce search space [48], but do not provide a systematic method to store and use these insights. Therefore, in this work, we propose a universal format to store and use expert insights for transistor sizing. 3.3 AMSgen Workflow The support from AMSnet enables the full automation of AMS circuit design, transition- ing from performance specifications to fully sized netlists. This section explores our LLM- assisted, data-driven design pipeline, AMSgen, as illustrated in Fig. 3.1. Section 3.3.1 de- tails the topology generation step. Section 3.3.2 discusses the sizing step, and Section 3.3.3 addresses the topology regeneration step in cases where the initial topology fails to meet performance goals after sizing. The user provides only the performance specifications and 32

En- gineers draw on their experience or additional resources to identify circuit topologies that meet the design goals and select testbenches to evaluate each performance metric. However, this process is labor-intensive, time-consuming, and heavily reliant on experience, making it challenging to automate. With the LLM technology available today, coupled with our AMSnet data support, we can fully automate this process and achieve the same goals. Given a set of performance metrics, AMSgen initially obtains a design strategy from the LLM that outlines the circuit architecture as a collection of subcircuits. It then retrieves corresponding subcircuits and testbenches from AMSnet before assembling them for simulation. Since the subcircuits are pre-validated, this ensures correctness, even when the LLM response is incorrect. State-of-the-art LLMs possess the knowledge needed to provide design strategies for de- sired circuits. However, they typically respond in natural text, which may be challenging to extract and use programmatically. To standardize the response format, we manually select an ICL example from a circuit sample set, encouraging the LLM to emulate this output for- mat, which facilitates further application of the response. To prevent the LLM from favoring any specific topology, the ICL examples describe different circuit types to provide formatting guidance only. For instance, we use a comparator design strategy as the few-shot example to generate OPAMPs, and vice versa. We also employ chain of thought (CoT) prompting methods, which have been shown to effectively enhance LLM performance. Specifically, the model is instructed by the example to first qualitatively analyze the requirements in the specifications and explain a thought process before providing the actual circuit design. Al- though the state-of-the-art LLM can produce reasonable design strategies without ICL or CoT, using these methods significantly improves formatting robustness. In an ideal scenario, the LLM would be capable of designing the entire circuit topology 34
