text: matches the feature Gain. We count the number of word occurrences on both sides, all in lowercase. The relation dm gain contains the word dm once and gain once, while the feature gain contains the word dm zero times and gain once. We compare the two vectors [1,1] and [0,1] to obtain a Hamming distance of 1. Similarly, we compare the label high against the value very high and obtain a Hamming distance of 1 as well, for a total distance of 2. We rank all matches in ascending order by this distance; the lowest distances have the minimal differences and therefore the closest match. Although this naive matching algorithm works well in our experiments, to enhance robustness, we could replace it with more sophisticated methods, such as language vector similarity or LLM inquiry. Now that we have both the block-level netlist and the corresponding subcircuits, AMSgen automatically references the matching circuits and joins the netlists to form the complete circuit. This process builds a fully functional netlist for simulation and prepares us for the upcoming sizing step. Currently, AMSnet contains only two block-level netlists, one for differential-input single-output OPAMPs and another for fully differential OPAMPs. As we expand into larger circuit types, there will be more block-level circuits to choose from. We will then resort to knowledge graph retrieval, similar to how we retrieve the subcircuits, to select the appropriate block-level netlists. 3.3.2 Constraint-Augmented Sizing Now that the circuit and test benches are fixed, the next step is to optimize component parameters to achieve maximum performance with the given topology. Sizing is formulated as a black-box optimization problem and is resolved through Bayesian optimization (BO) with local annotations retrieved from AMSnet. 37

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: Problem Formulation: We present the standard constrained optimization problem in Equation 3.1: maximize FoM(x) s.t. gj(x) ≤ 0, ∀j ∈ {1, . . . , p} (3.1) where the figure of merits (FoM) is the objective function, and gj(x) is the j-th performance constraint. Following [43, 49], we define FoM as the weighted square sum of the normalized performance value, as shown in Equation 3.2: FoM = N X i=0 wi × min(fi(x), fbound i ) − fmin i fmax i − fmin i (3.2) where fi(x) is i-th simulated performance, fbound i is the performance limit above which we do not get additional merit, fmin i and fmax i are normalization factors obtained through an initial set of random samples, and wi is the term weight to control the importance of each performance metric. Bayesian optimization (BO) is a strategy for global optimization, particularly suitable for optimizing black-box functions. It is usually employed when the function evaluation is expensive or the search space is too large to exhaust. BO treats the black-box function to be optimized as a stochastic process, typically modeled using a Gaussian Process (GP) as a surrogate model. The GP provides a flexible way to describe the distribution of the black-box function and updates predictions based on existing data points. By sampling initial data points, the GP model is trained to fit the black-box function. An acquisition function is selected to balance exploration and exploitation, determining the next sampling point. In the input space, the point that maximizes the acquisition function is found. The selected new point is then evaluated through simulation, and its result is added to the existing dataset, updating the GP model. By balancing exploration and exploitation, BO can avoid getting trapped in local optima and find the global optimum. 38

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: Gaussian Process: A GP is a stochastic process defined over an input space, where any finite subset of random variables follows a multivariate Gaussian distribution. Given a training dataset {(xi, yi)}n i=1, where xi are the inputs and yi are the target values. A GP is completely defined by its mean function µ(x) and covariance function k(x, x′ ). The mean function represents the expected value of the function at a given input, and the covariance function (also called the kernel function) represents the correlation or similarity between any two points. Generally, the mean function of a GP is assumed to be zero: m(x) = E[f(x)] = 0 (3.3) The kernel function k(x, x′ ) is defined as: k(x, x′ ) = E[(f(x) − m(x))(f(x′ ) − m(x′ ))] (3.4) For a new input point x∗, the predictive distribution is also a Gaussian distribution. The mean and variance of the prediction can be computed as follows: µ∗ = k(x∗, X)T K−1 y (3.5) σ2 ∗ = k(x∗, x∗) − k(x∗, X)T K−1 k(x∗, X) (3.6) where k(x∗, X) is the covariance vector between the new input point and all training data points, and y is the vector of target values for the training data. Acquisition Function: The acquisition function is a key component in BO, used to se- lect the next evaluation point. It balances exploration and exploitation, making trade-offs between exploring unknown regions to gain knowledge and exploiting the best-known regions to find optima. Expected Improvement (EI) : EI measures the expected amount of improvement over the current best point. The formula is: αEI(x) = E[max(0, f(x) − f(x+ ))] (3.7) 39

text: where f(x+ ) is the current best observed value. By modeling our custom FoM as a black-box function of the design parameters, we are able to use a GP to fit the simulation and use BO to optimize our parameters without explicit knowledge. Sizing Constraints: Exhaustively searching parameters for all transistors is inefficient; therefore, expert insights stored in local annotations serve as constraints to reduce the pa- rameter search space. For instance, with the annotation that a set of transistor parameters should maintain equality or a certain ratio, they share the same parameter with some con- stant multiplier to match the ratio. The algorithm flow for constraint-augmented sizing is as follows: 3.3.3 Topology Regeneration In the case where an initial topology design does not satisfy the desired metrics after a set amount of sizing effort, it is considered a topology issue, and the design flow proceeds to a topology regeneration step. The topology regeneration process is very similar to the initial topology design process. The only difference is that, instead of using a different circuit application in the few-shot examples, here the actual performance specifications obtained from the previous designs are used to give the LLM additional quantitative knowledge. With the previous design strategy proposed by the LLM and the optimal performance during simulation, the design flow essentially reverses the cause-effect and pretends that it initially wanted to achieve the performance metrics, and then correctly obtained the previous design. For example, suppose that an OPAMP with a DM gain of 60 dB is initially required, the LLM initially proposed a design strategy to retrieve circuit components and assemble circuit A. Then the process outlined in section 3.3.2 is applied, and finally ended with a fully sized design that only achieves a DM gain of 40 dB. This approach is especially effective since initially the state-of-the-art LLM does not pos- sess sufficient quantitative knowledge. It is unable to accurately infer the performance of a specific circuit topology on a specific technology node, and therefore generally begins with a balanced design that has no particular weakness. However, it does possess qualitative and comparative knowledge between different topologies, as they generally hold across all tech- nology nodes. In this example where we require a higher gain, it is often able to correctly suggest a new topology that specializes in higher gain. text: 3.5 Discussions In this chapter, we introduced AMSgen, a fully automated, data-driven framework for ana- log and mixed-signal (AMS) circuit generation, built upon the AMSnet dataset. AMSgen leverages large language models (LLMs) to emulate the decision-making process of expe- rienced engineers, utilizing our knowledge graph for topological retrieval and assembly. It further employs Bayesian optimization to derive optimal device sizing, completing the de- sign flow from high-level performance specifications to fully sized netlists without any human intervention beyond the initial input. Experimental results demonstrate AMSgen’s ability to generate complex circuits such as operational amplifiers and comparators that meet all specified performance targets. These results validate the feasibility and effectiveness of our modular approach that separates topology construction from sizing and simulation, while incorporating expert knowledge through structured annotations. Despite these promising outcomes, several challenges remain. First, the Bayesian op- timization process becomes computationally intensive as circuit complexity increases. For larger systems, thousands of simulations may be required, leading to prohibitive runtime if performed naively. The next chapter addresses this by introducing a divide-and-conquer approach, using a SAR ADC design as a case study to scale AMSgen to more complex circuits. Second, current experiments rely exclusively on pre-layout simulations, which omit par- asitic effects. This limits the accuracy of the sizing results in post-fabrication conditions. However, recent advances in automated layout generation, such as abuttable analog cells (Acells) [51], offer a path toward integrating post-layout simulations into the optimization loop. Future work will incorporate automated layout generation to ensure that parasitics are accounted for during sizing. Finally, AMSgen currently depends on preset testbench topologies for simulation, which 53

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: constrains the diversity of circuits and metrics that can be evaluated. To overcome this limitation, future work will explore LLM-driven generation of testbenches, including both topology and metric extraction code, thereby expanding the range of supported circuit types and performance evaluations. Overall, AMSgen marks a significant step toward fully autonomous AMS circuit design, demonstrating that LLMs, when grounded in domain-specific data and augmented with structured engineering knowledge, can drive meaningful progress in analog EDA automa- tion. 54

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: CHAPTER 4 Automated SAR ADC Design Using Analytic Equations 4.1 Introduction Analog-to-digital converters (ADCs), connecting analog sensors to digital processing, have become an essential IP in most System on Chips (SoCs). Successive Approximation Register (SAR) ADCs, with applications ranging from medium-low precision to ultra-high-speed de- signs, have attracted significant attention [52, 53, 54]. However, conventional design meth- ods primarily rely on manual adjustments. As technology nodes shrink and design com- plexity grows exponentially, manually designing SAR ADCs has become increasingly time- consuming. This inefficient design process struggles to meet the demands of a fast-evolving market, necessitating an automatic design methodology. Device sizing is a crucial step in the design flow of analog and mixed-signal (AMS) in- tegrated circuits, such as SAR ADC. Previous work on automatic sizing can be broadly classified into knowledge-based and optimization-based approaches. Knowledge-based ap- proaches rely on analytic equations to derive circuit performance and device sizing, usu- ally involving assumptions and approximations with various empirical values. In contrast, optimization-based approaches depend on trials and errors in the simulation environments and are very time-consuming. Significant research effort [52, 43, 55, 56] has been dedicated to automating optimization-based methods using machine learning (ML) algorithms such as Bayesian optimization (BO) and reinforcement learning (RL). However, these methods are 55

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: Figure 4.1: Automated Design Framework Overview often limited to small-scale circuits, such as OPAMP or comparator designs within twenty transistors. Due to the extensive parameter search spaces and high simulation costs, only a few studies [57, 58, 59] have been extended to larger ones, such as ADCs. On the other hand, there have been some pioneering knowledge-based automatic sizing [20], but again the circuit scale is limited. There have been research achievements on automatic sizing of SAR ADCs. However, the proposed methods typically require human interventions within the optimization loop. This demands professional SAR-ADC-specific knowledge, and could potentially introduce human errors. [57, 58] both achieve some level of automation in SAR ADC design. However, [57] still requires a human expert to determine the priority of device sizing. [58] needs a pre- characterized comparator library of different device parameters, which is time-consuming to obtain. To address the above challenges, this chapter proposes an automated system-level de- sign methodology for SAR ADCs, as illustrated in Fig. 4.1. The overall motivation is to make use of numerous analytical equations that maps performance from complex circuits to its simpler subcircuits, where latter are usually within reach of popular automated sizing frameworks. The tool requires only high-level performance specifications as input, and the built-in library will supply the circuit topology, testbenches, and analytical equations, facil- 56

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: itating automatic generation of complete SAR ADC netlists without human intervention. It begins with an equation processing phase, during which a dependency graph is constructed from the analytical equations to establish a topological order for simulations for verifica- tion, knowledge-based calculations and optimization-based transistor sizing. Based on the dependency graph, we integrate a dual optimization scheme to address the high-dimensional transistor sizing optimization problem in SAR ADCs. The system-level optimization iter- atively decomposes the overall performance specifications into individual subcircuits, while several local optimization loops employ BO to optimize the transistor parameters of the subcircuits. The locally optimized results of the subcircuits are then fed back to the system level for overall performance simulation or calculation. Finally, the loop concludes once all constraints are satisfied, yielding the complete device sizing for the SAR ADC. Our contributions are as follows. • We propose a fully-automated SAR ADC design methodology that generates optimized device sizing directly from performance specifications. The dependency graph-based framework is proposed to serialize the simulations for verification, knowledge-based calculations, and transistor sizing optimization in topological order. • We utilize a dual optimization scheme to tackle the high-dimensional sizing prob- lem. The system-level optimization iteratively decomposes the overall performance specifications into individual subcircuits, while local optimization loops employ BO to optimize the transistor parameters of the subcircuits. This ensures that both overall performance goals and individual subcircuit constraints are met efficiently. • We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through two case studies with varying performance specifications. 57

text: 4.2 Preliminaries This section introduces the background knowledge of SAR ADCs including the key design considerations. We also provide a brief overview of Bayesian optimization (BO), the machine learning algorithm employed to optimize device parameters and empirical values. 4.2.1 SAR ADC Architecture Fig. 4.2 shows a typical SAR ADC architecture. The functionality of each subcircuit is listed below. • Bootstrap Sample-and-Hold Switch (SWS/H): Captures and stores the input voltage during the sampling phase to provide a stable input signal for conversion. • Capacitive Digital-to-Analog Converter (CDAC): Converts the digital code from the SAR logic into an analog voltage for comparison. • Pre-amplifier: Amplifies the input signal to a desired level, enhancing accuracy and minimizing noise before comparison. • Comparator: Compares the CDAC outputs and generates a digital decision. • SAR Logic: Controls the iterative conversion process, adjusting the CDAC and com- parator settings to produce the final digital output. The main performance metrics of the SAR ADC usually include resolution N, sampling frequency fs, power consumption, and area. 4.2.2 Bayesian Optimization Eq. 4.1 describes an abstract optimization problem, where we seek to maximize a certain objective function F(x) by tuning the input variables x, subject to a series of p constraints 58

In the context of device sizing, F(x) is typically defined by some performance metrics, where each gj(x) describes the legal search space of a certain parameter, usually set by the PDK or prior knowledge. maximize F(x) s.t. gj(x) ≤ 0, ∀j ∈ {1, . . . , p} (4.1) Bayesian optimization uses a machine learning model, typically a Gaussian process, as the surrogate model to represent the true relationship between the input parameters and the output objective function. The optimization process is iterative; in each iteration, it interacts with the unknown function F(x) with some input x carefully chosen by its acquisition function, and uses the output to update the surrogate model. After sufficient iterations, it is expected to converge to a sufficiently strong objective. 4.3 Algorithms In this section, we introduce the algorithms in the proposed optimization framework shown in Fig. 4.6. This is accomplished through metric mapping, where the performance specifications of the complete design are analyt- ically translated into the specifications for each individual subcircuit. Each subcircuit is then optimized independently and, once finalized, integrated into the full SAR ADC for performance verification. Section 4.3.1 first formulates the problem with the overall and subcircuit-level perfor- mance requirements into variables and relations. Section 4.3.2 presents the dependency graph used to first partition specifications to subcircuits, then serialize the analytical cal- culation, subcircuit optimization, and constraint verification steps. Section 4.3.3 describes how BO is applied in two distinct contexts: subcircuit-level BO to optimize individual subcircuits and system-level BO to optimize the overall design. 4.3.1 Subcircuit Design Specifications In the architecture shown in Fig. 4.2, the subcircuits we assume are presented in Fig. 4.3. As shown in Table 4.1, each variable may appear on either side of a relation; however, we ensure that only a single variable appears on the left-hand side (LHS). This establishes a dependency from the LHS variable to all variables on the right-hand side (RHS). By considering variables as nodes and dependencies as edges, we construct a dependency graph (see Fig. 4.7 for a partial example). In this work, to simplify the problem, we assume that the dependency graph is cycle-free. Consequently, the graph satisfies the properties of a directed acyclic graph (DAG). This property enables topological sorting, which guarantees that all RHS variables are evaluated before their corresponding LHS expressions are computed or verified. A subcircuit’s performance specifications are derived once all related constraints are 65

text: Figure 4.7: Dependency graph example, variables and equations are explained in detail in Fig. 4.6 evaluated through dependency graph propagation. This effectively partitions the system- level performance specifications to subcircuits. The flow then performs subcircuit-level BO on the subcircuit individually to meet the corresponding specifications. After obtaining simulation results for constraint verification, the flow propagates the performance metrics down the dependency graph in topological order to compute constraints for other subcircuits. For instance, as described in Section 4.3.1, the comparator offset Vos is used to set a constraint on the preamplifier gain AV . In this way, subcircuit-level optimization, simulation, and constraint verification are serialized. 4.3.3 Optimization Procedure As shown in Fig. 4.6, BO drives the main optimization efforts in this work. After generating the dependency graph, we employ a system-level optimization loop to obtain a set of empirical values that balance performance and feasibility. The loop terminates when either all constraints are satisfied or the maximum number of iterations is reached. In practice, as demonstrated in Section 4.4, all constraints are met within a single iteration of system-level 66

If any subcir- cuit performance metric fails to meet its constraint, the deviation is incorporated into the system-level BO loss. In the 14-bit 500 KS/s design, 62% of the power consumption is attributed to the SAR logic. This is due to the higher power consumption associated with the use of synchronous SAR logic. The power consumption might be further optimized if asynchronous SAR was used. In the 12-bit 1 MS/s design, the power consumption of comparator accounts for a larger proportion of the total power consumption, as the dynamic power of the comparator rises in high-speed designs. In terms of optimization efficiency, as we increase the desired ADC resolution from 12 to 14 and reduce sampling frequency from 1M to 500k, we notice a change in runtime. The comparator requires fewer iterations to meet specifications, while the bootstrap circuit and the pre-amplifier take longer. This is because the higher resolution requirement sets harder specifications for the bootstrap and pre-amplifier circuits. Overall, the proposed framework arrives at a similar FoM and runtime to the previous work, showing the effectiveness of the automated method even without manual intervention. 4.5 Discussion and Future Work In this work, we propose an autonomous SAR ADC sizing framework. We construct a dependency graph from predefined analytical equations, then use the topological order of the graph to serialize a system-level optimization loop. Within the loop, we partition system-level specifications to each subcircuit and optimize them individually. Finally, the flow verifies the design constraints and decides whether to continue the optimization loop. We verified the proposed framework on two different sets of performance specifications, and successfully produced functional SAR ADCs with comparable performance to previous autonomous sizing frameworks. For future work, our method will be improved on three different fronts. Firstly, the acyclic 69

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: dependency assumption will be released, which allows us to support any set of analytical equations. Next, we will employ offline sizing methods, where the subcircuit-level BO are performed from pre-collected simulation data, so that we pay a one-time cost for all sizing, and therefore runtime no longer scales linearly with the number of system-level iterations. This should allow us to tackle less thoroughly collected equations and more aggressive em- pirical value ranges. Finally, we will expand our method to different types of circuits, as the current methodology is not designed specifically for SAR ADCs and may work for other hierarchical AMS designs as well. 70

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: CHAPTER 5 Conclusion This dissertation presents a comprehensive, data-driven approach to automating analog/mixed- signal (AMS) circuit analysis and design. By addressing the longstanding challenges in AMS design—namely its reliance on manual effort, lack of explainability, and resistance to automa- tion—we introduce a series of novel methodologies and systems that collectively move the field closer to fully automated design workflows. We began by developing AMSnet, a multimodal database of schematics, netlists, and functional annotations. This dataset was made possible through a robust schematic parsing pipeline that combines traditional algorithms and machine learning techniques to reliably convert circuit images into structured netlists. The annotated data and knowledge graph organization of AMSnet provide rich, queryable insights that support downstream design tasks. Building upon this foundation, we introduced AMSgen, an LLM-assisted design frame- work that autonomously translates performance specifications into complete circuit designs. AMSgen integrates natural language reasoning, knowledge graph retrieval, and Bayesian op- timization in a feedback loop, enabling it to generate and refine topologies and device sizing without human intervention. This framework successfully produced designs for operational amplifiers and comparators, with layout-aware optimization through analog cell libraries (Acells). To address the scalability limitations of simulation-heavy optimization, we proposed a hierarchical design flow for complex systems like SAR ADCs. By decomposing global speci- 71

title: Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuit Analysis and Design: A Data-Driven Approach (thesis, includes AMSgen)
text: fications into local targets and coordinating subcircuit optimization via dependency graphs, we significantly reduced computational overhead. This allowed for efficient end-to-end design of circuits with over 200 devices—without requiring full-circuit simulation in each iteration. Together, these contributions demonstrate that combining LLMs, computer vision, struc- tured datasets, and analytical reasoning can unlock practical solutions to AMS design au- tomation. Our work bridges the gap between tacit expert knowledge and formalized compu- tational models, offering new capabilities for both academia and industry. Looking forward, several promising research directions emerge: Testbench Generation: Automatically creating simulation setups for evaluating circuit performance would remove one of the last remaining manual steps in the design pipeline. Self-supervised Annotation: Developing tools to automatically annotate functionality, symmetry constraints, and performance traits would further reduce the human cost of dataset expansion. Improved Multimodal Understanding: Enhancing LLMs with native schematic interpre- tation—possibly through fine-tuning with AMSnet—could lead to models capable of directly parsing and generating circuit diagrams. Design Debugging and Explainability: Integrating diagnostic tools that can explain de- sign failures or suggest corrective actions would make the design process more transparent and trustworthy. Broader Circuit Coverage: Extending the framework to handle more circuit classes such as filters, oscillators, and power management blocks would expand its applicability. In conclusion, this dissertation sets the stage for the next generation of AMS design tools—ones that are data-driven, intelligent, and capable of emulating the decision-making processes of expert designers. By continuing to expand the dataset, refine the automation algorithms, and deepen the integration with domain knowledge, we envision a future where complex AMS design can be performed quickly, accurately, and autonomously. 72

DC Gain (> 80dB): The requirement for a high DC gain indicates that the op-amp should have multiple stages to ensure a high level of amplification. A cascaded configuration can be used, typically starting with a differential input stage for high gain and good common-mode rejection. 2. Gain-Bandwidth Product (GBW > 10MHz): This necessitates a design that balances gain and frequency response. A compensation technique, like Miller compensation, might be employed in the gain stage to extend the bandwidth while maintaining stability. 3. Phase Margin (> 60 degrees): To achieve a stable operation with a phase margin greater than 60 degrees, careful design of the feedback network and internal compensation are required. This involves selecting appropriate capacitor values for the compensation network to ensure that the phase shift does not lead to instability. 4. Common-Mode Rejection Ratio (CMRR > 80dB): A high CMRR is crucial for reducing noise and interference that appears commonly on both inputs. This can be achieved by ensuring that the input stage has highly matched transistors and by using techniques such as common-mode feedback. 5. Power Supply Rejection Ratio (PSRR > 80dB): To achieve high PSRR, the power supply lines should be well decoupled. Additionally, using a differential architecture throughout can help minimize the effect of supply variations on the output. Circuit Structure: Input Stage: ● Differential Pair: Utilize a differential pair with NMOS transistors for the input stage to achieve high input impedance and initial gain. This stage will be the primary contributor to the CMRR. ● Active Load: Employ an active load (typically a current mirror) to convert the differential input signal into a single-ended output while increasing the gain. Gain Stage: ● Second Stage (Voltage Gain Stage): A second amplification stage can further amplify the signal from the input stage. This stage typically uses a PMOS transistor for high gain and can be configured with Miller compensation to stabilize the gain and bandwidth. Compensation and Stability: ● Miller Compensation: Implement Miller compensation across the second stage to control the frequency response and stabilize the op-amp by increasing the phase margin. Speed and Power Optimization: ● Optimized Transistor Sizing: Use minimum size for the input differential pair to minimize parasitic capacitances, enhancing the speed. Carefully size the transistors in the input and gain stages to optimize the trade-off between speed, gain, and power consumption. ● Biasing: Efficiently bias all stages to ensure that the op-amp operates within the power constraints while maintaining linearity and minimizing power dissipation. This approach will meet the stringent requirements set out for the operational amplifier in a 28nm CMOS process, achieving a balance between performance parameters and practical design constraints. A common approach is to employ a two-stage architecture, beginning with a differential input stage, which provides substantial initial gain and excellent common-mode rejection capabilities. 2. Gain-Bandwidth Product (GBW > 10 MHz): To meet this requirement while maintaining a high DC gain, it is essential to use frequency compensation techniques such as Miller compensation in the second gain stage. This helps in achieving a wide bandwidth without sacrificing stability. 3. Phase Margin (> 60 degrees): Ensuring a phase margin greater than 60 degrees is crucial for the stability of the op-amp. This can be achieved by careful design of the compensation network, possibly incorporating a Miller capacitor that connects the output of the second stage back to an intermediate stage. 4. Common-Mode Rejection Ratio (CMRR > 80 dB): High CMRR is essential for applications requiring accuracy and noise immunity. This can be achieved by utilizing well-matched transistor pairs in the differential input stage and employing techniques like common-mode feedback to enhance symmetry. 5. Power Supply Rejection Ratio (PSRR > 80 dB): High PSRR is achieved by minimizing the impact of power supply fluctuations on the amplifier’s output. This involves the use of regulated supply voltages and integrating a rejection mechanism such as differential stages throughout the design to reject common-mode signals from the power supply. Circuit Structure: Input Stage: ● Differential Pair: Use a differential pair with NMOS transistors for the input to achieve high input impedance and significant initial gain. Gain Stage: ● Second Stage (Voltage Gain Stage): A second amplification stage will further amplify the signal from the input stage. This stage typically uses a PMOS transistor for improved gain characteristics and is where Miller compensation can be applied. Compensation and Stability: ● Miller Compensation: Implement Miller compensation across the second stage. This method involves connecting a compensation capacitor between the output and an intermediate point (usually the gate of a transistor in the first stage), effectively controlling the frequency response and stabilizing the op-amp by increasing the phase margin. This often involves selecting appropriate values for the compensation capacitors and possibly incorporating additional poles or zeros strategically. CMRR > 80dB and PSRR > 80dB: Both requirements point towards a need for excellent matching and symmetry in the differential input stage and minimizing supply and common-mode noise influence. Techniques like using matched transistor pairs and common centroid layout can help improve CMRR and PSRR. Gain Stage (Second Stage): Common-Source Stage with Active Load: The second stage can be a common-source amplifier driven by the output of the first stage. This stage further amplifies the voltage and drives the output load. Another PMOS can be used as the active load to further improve the gain. Compensation: Place a compensation capacitor and a resistor between the output of the first stage and the output of the second stage to stabilize the two-stage amplifier configuration and set the dominant pole for desired phase margin and bandwidth. Speed and Stability Optimization: Minimize Parasitic Effects: use minimum length for transistors where possible to reduce parasitic capacitances, enhancing speed. title: An LLM-assisted Analog IC Design Tool with Automatic Topology Selection and Circuit Sizing
text: An LLM-assisted Analog IC Design Tool with Automatic Topology Selection and Circuit Sizing Anh Nguyen, Chien-Nan Jimmy Liu {EECS International Graduate Program, Institute of Electronics} National Yang-Ming Chiao Tung University Hsinchu City, Taiwan, R.O.C. {nta.ee12, jimmyliu}@nycu.edu.tw Abstract—Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained a rising interest in different domains, including code generation for digital IC design. However, building an effective LLM for analog IC design is challenging because a valid analog circuit cannot be constructed by just randomly combining some codes. In this paper, an LLM-assisted analog IC design tool is presented to support from automatic topology selection to circuit sizing in a conversational manner. This tool allows designers to express their requirements through natural language rather than being restricted by a fixed template, which decreases the learning curve of using such an automation tool. In order to meet users’ intentions, a subsequent ANN-based sizing process is invoked to further refine the “nearest” circuit obtained from the LLM without tedious iterations. Compared with previous works, the proposed LLM-assisted tool is more efficient and convenient while generating reliable analog designs to meet users’ requirements. Our experiments show that the tool can generate workable circuits with short execution time. Keywords—LLM, Zero-shot-CoT prompting, kNN search, automatic circuit sizing, ANN, circuit topology selection I. INTRODUCTION Because traditional analog IC design flow heavily relies on past knowledge and intuition, analog design automation has been studied for years to alleviate the long design cycles [1]. Most of existing works require a given circuit topology from designers, which still needs some prior knowledge to make a proper selection. A topology searching method in collaboration with a subsequent sizing process performed on a pre-built circuit library was proposed [4]. However, using decision tree traversal for topology selection often results in a long execution time when the number of candidates increases [4][14]. Further, [4] cannot take advantage of massive parallelism of graphics processing units (GPUs). Another approach uses artificial neural networks (ANNs) to merge topology selection and circuit sizing into one step, thus reducing the overall execution time [15]. Nevertheless, due to the uncertainty of ANN classification, inconsistent topology selection can occur under the same specification when users query at different time. This can be further exacerbated as the number of classification nodes increases. Therefore, it is important to find a good tradeoff between execution time and accuracy to be adopted by industrial designers. Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently gained attention in Design Automation field because they allow IC designers to “discuss with an assistant” to construct a circuit. Thus, they can enable IC design tasks to become more easy and convenient without too much prior training. Despite a significant progress made in digital domain [2][13], the potential of LLMs in analog domain remains underdeveloped. Digital IC design automation can be thought of as a process of code generation and evaluation, safely ignoring effect of transistor sizes. However, due to the multifaceted constraints of analog ICs, building an effective LLM for analog IC design is more challenging because a valid analog circuit cannot be constructed by just randomly combining some codes. A recent work trains an LLM from both valid and invalid circuits to generate different topologies for analog designs with random performance [3]. In this approach, the randomly generated circuits are not guaranteed to be workable under the given specification, which is not acceptable for industrial designers. In practical applications, a reliable design tool is often desired. To utilize previous design experience, combining LLM with a trustworthy circuit library might be a good choice to help analog circuit design automation. In this paper, we present an LLM-assisted analog IC (AIC) design tool that supports from automatic topology selection to circuit sizing in a conversational manner. Designers can express their requirements through natural language rather than being restricted by a fixed template, which decreases the learning curve of using such an automation tool. Based on an extendable circuit library, the proposed LLM-based topology selection is guided by Zero-shot-Chain-of-Thought (Zero- shot-CoT) prompting and k-nearest neighbors (kNN) search to achieve an extremely short execution time on getting a feasible solution from the trustworthy candidates. This approach is able to maintain reliable solutions at each usage iteration, which is more acceptable by analog designers. However, it is impossible to prepare all solutions in advance to meet any user’s request. Therefore, to meet the user’s intentions, a subsequent ANN-based sizing process is invoked to further refine the “nearest” circuit obtained from the library without tedious iterations. Compared with previous analog design automation approaches, the proposed LLM-assisted tool is more efficient and convenient while generating reliable analog designs to meet users’ requirements. II. The topology and corresponding device sizes of this design will form the design context to answer the user’s query. If the question requires some details of past conversations, the historical context is formed by retrieving relevant information from the chat log, which is then concatenated with the design context to form the total context for the final answer. Trustworthy Circuit Library There are 12 circuit “feature names” in our trustworthy circuit library: gain, phase margin, unity frequency, bandwidth, dynamic power (with a 100kHz square wave input), static power, slew rate, estimated area, common mode rejection ratio (CMRR), power supply rejection ratio (PSRR), bias current, capacitance load. The library consists of 25 commonly used operational transconductance amplifiers (OTAs) and operational amplifiers (OPAMPs). Because each row in the library pertains to a vector including specifications of all feature names with corresponding device sizes and device values of a particular topology, the term “Specification Table” is used in Fig. 1. Fig. 1. The tool’s workflow. Fig. 2. The tool’s GUI. D. Three-Stage Conversational Topology Selection The topology selection module is conceptually divided into 3 stages. The module utilizes a general-purpose LLM, namely Llama 3.1 8B Instruct [5], in collaboration with our searching and prompting techniques, to quickly opt for a circuit topology in a conversational manner. Three stages are sequentially called “Summarization”, “Retrieving k Circuits” and “Choosing Best-Matched”, as shown in Fig. 3. Fig. 3. Flowchart of the topology selection module. In the “Summarization” stage, if T numbers of feature names are queried, a “Summarization” prompt automatically constructs T questions, each starts with a sentence “what is the required value of”, followed by a feature name fc. The sentence “You have to answer in bullet points” also needs to be present. The LLM takes the user’s query and passes it through the “Summarization” prompt to generate a “Summary” in which the queried parameters are always arranged in the same order. This allows users to query about any circuit parameter in any order based on their thought processes. Furthermore, due to the LLM’s capability to handle spelling mistakes, incorrect feature names can be mended so that they are consistent with the circuit library. Fig .4 illustrates the process of making a “Summary” from a query. Fig. 4. The process of making a “Summary” from a query. The “Summary” is fed to the “Retrieving k Circuits” stage. Firstly, a regular expression parses the “Summary” to obtain a “Performance Mapping Sequence” denoted by: Sperf = {v1(f1), v2(f2), …, vT(fT)} (1) where v1(f1) is the first feature’s value, v2(f2) is the second feature’s value, etc. The final feature’s value is vT(fT) if there are T queried feature names. Secondly, a kNN search [7] is performed on the library to retrieve k nearest data vectors of the Sperf. Empirically, we set hyperparameter k=4 and utilize Euclidean Distance Metric in our tool. Thirdly, an “Unrolling” procedure transforms the k vectors into k paragraphs by starting each paragraph with our customized phrase “design log”, followed by a row index i, a “:” symbol, a feature name fc, a “=” symbol, and a feature value vc(fc). It makes a series of T descriptive pairs for each of the k resultant paragraphs. The kNN search is illustrated in Fig. 5. An example of the “Unrolling” procedure is illustrated in Fig. 6. As can be seen from Fig.7, the “Best-Matched” prompt is constructed by a concatenation of a fixed paragraph called “Request 1”, the k circuit paragraphs, another fixed paragraph called “Request 2”, and the original user’s query. As illustrated in Fig. 7, The LLM in our tool takes the “Best-Matched” prompt as an input to produce the best-matched design, which is a circuit with device sizes that satisfies a query. This design is also the output of the topology selection module. Fig. 7. Struture and functionality of the “Best-Matched” prompt. The purpose of the kNN search is to return several designs with shortest distances from a Sperf. It is more practical than returning only one vector because there would be cases where the design that aligns with a user’s intentions lies in a vector that is further away from a specific Sperf than the closest vector. For example, a vector V1={40dB,15kHz} is further away from a Sperf ={38dB,17kHz} than a vector V2={37dB,18kHz} but the query contains verbal conditions such as “gain>38dB”. Thus, Zero-shot-CoT prompting can collaborate with kNN search to obtain a more aligned result in such case. E. Automatic Circuit Sizing When a retrieved circuit does not meet the requirement, a subsequent sizing can be performed. ANN-based sizing is suitable in our case because of 2 reasons. Firstly, data from the library is reused in our training process. Secondly, because no new topology is added in the current version of the tool, sizing an existing circuit with a predetermined target from a query can take advantage of the extremely fast inference time of ANNs. We adopt the sizing method featuring ANNs from [8] with 2 major changes. In [8], error metrics are mean absolute error (MAE) and mean squared error (MSE). Both MSE and MAE decrease in the training process to approach zero without definitive ratios. Thus, R-Square Score (R2-score) [9] is an addition in our work to increase the interpretability of the results. As MSE decreases, R2-score approaches 1.0 (a ratio), meaning that the error between actual and predicted data is gradually minimized in training and evaluation. Another departure from [8] is that polynomial features are not utilized because we have not observed any improvement as compared to the case where only original data are used. F. Information Retrieval from Chat Log A chat log is integrated so that users can query about the conversation history. To achieve the correct contexts from the chat log, instead of relying on dense retrieval [10], we employ a sparse retriever based on BM25 algorithm [11] for 2 reasons. Firstly, as the log becomes lengthier, creating a dense embedding vector of the whole log is significantly slower than calculating BM25 index. Secondly, sparse retrieval permits exact term matches which is important in searching for technical terms. This is pointed out in [12]. A hybrid retriever, a combination of a sparse retriever and a dense retriever, can also be discarded due to its slow runtime. III. title: Large Language Models for EDA: Future or Mirage?
text: Large Language Models for EDA: Future or Mirage? ZHUOLUN HE, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, Hong Kong YUAN PU, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, Hong Kong HAOYUAN WU, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, Hong Kong TAIRU QIU, ChatEDA Tech, Foshan, China BEI YU, CSE, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, Hong Kong In this article, we explore the burgeoning intersection of large language models (LLMs) and electronic design automation (EDA). We critically assess whether LLMs represent a transformative future for EDA or merely a fleeting mirage. By organizing existing research into four critical domains of EDA—code generation, verification and debugging, knowledge representation and retrieval, and optimization/modeling—we provide a comprehensive overview of the current state-of-the-art. The survey concludes with a 5-level roadmap to guide the progressive integration and advancement of LLMs in EDA. Ultimately, this article aims to provide a comprehensive, evidence-based perspective on the role of LLMs in shaping the future of EDA. text: 90:2 Z. He et al. limitations of these conventional methods, such as long design cycles, high costs, and the need for extensive human expertise, underscore the necessity for new approaches. Concurrently, the field of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML), has witnessed remarkable progress. Large Language Models (LLMs), a subset of ML, have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in understanding and generating human-like text. This success has sparked interest in applying LLMs to a wide array of domains, including EDA, where they can potentially address some of the most pressing challenges faced by the industry. LLMs [1–4] are sophisticated AI systems that are trained on vast datasets of text and code, enabling them to perform a wide range of natural language processing tasks [5–8]. In the context of EDA, LLM for EDA refers to the application of LLMs to various stages of the electronic design process, from initial architectural exploration to detailed physical design and post-silicon validation. The primary objective of LLM for EDA is to leverage the powerful language processing and pattern recognition capabilities of LLMs to enhance the efficiency, accuracy, and automation of EDA workflows. The integration of LLMs into EDA holds significant potential for transforming the way chips are designed. By automating repetitive and labor-intensive tasks, LLMs can accelerate the design process, reduce the likelihood of human error, and free up engineers to focus on more creative and strategic aspects of design. For example, LLMs can assist in generating and optimizing hardware descriptions, performing design space explorations, and even aiding in the debugging and verification of complex designs. Moreover, LLMs can provide a more intuitive and user-friendly interface, allowing designers to interact with EDA tools using natural language. This could democratize access to advanced EDA capabilities, making it easier for non-experts to engage in the design process. Additionally, the ability of LLMs to learn from large datasets and adapt to specific tasks through fine-tuning offers the potential for highly customized and optimized design solutions. This survey provides a rigorous exploration of the integration of LLMs into four critical domains of EDA: code generation, verification and debugging, knowledge representation and retrieval, and optimization/modeling. These categories reflect the broad capabilities of LLMs in addressing critical challenges throughout the design and development pipeline. Code generation focuses on the automated synthesis of hardware description languages (HDLs), system-level designs, analog circuits, high-level synthesis (HLS), and flow scripts, significantly accelerating prototyping and reducing manual effort. Verification and debugging encompass the use of LLMs to ensure design correctness, detect and resolve errors, and validate functionality and security through tasks like testbench generation, assertion synthesis, fault localization, and bug fixing. Knowledge representation and retrieval leverages LLMs to encode, retrieve, and reason over vast amounts of design-related data, enabling efficient specification analysis, bug classification, and question answering (QA) to support informed decision-making. Finally, optimization/modeling focuses on improving key design metrics such as power, performance, and area (PPA) by employing LLMs for tasks like circuit sizing, layout refinement, and workflow automation. This taxonomy not only underscores the versatility of LLMs in tackling various stages of the design flow but also elucidates the potential for improved designer productivity, enhanced design quality, and accelerated innovation. Figure 1 illustrates some of the covered topics of this survey, centered around four principal axes of modality transformation: code-to-code, code-to-language, language-to-code, and language-to- language. The space is divided into four quadrants, respectively, named as the compilation quadrant (C2C), the codegen quadrant (NL2C), the chatbot quadrant (NL2NL), and the modeling quadrant (C2NL). Each axis represents a distinct approach to leveraging LLMs’ prowess in interpreting and generating information, thereby bridging the gap between the abstract concepts of human intent and the concrete realities of hardware implementation. LLMs are reshaping EDA practices, from automating low-level coding tasks to enabling high-level design specification through natural language commands. 2 Preliminary 2.1 EDA EDA is a category of software tools used for designing and verifying electronic systems, including ICs, printed circuit boards (PCBs), and other complex electronic components. EDA tools are essential for the semiconductor industry, enabling designers to create, simulate, and verify the functionality and performance of electronic designs before they are manufactured. The importance of EDA lies in its ability to manage the increasing complexity of modern electronic systems, reduce design time, and ensure that designs meet stringent PPA requirements. EDA involves a comprehensive and iterative workflow that transforms high-level specifications into physical chip designs [9, 10]. The EDA process begins with the specification and architecture phase, where the system’s functional requirements, performance targets, and constraints are defined. This is followed by the HLS or register-transfer level (RTL) design, in which the architectural specifications are translated into an HDL that represents the digital circuit at a higher abstraction level. Logic synthesis then converts the RTL code into a gate-level netlist, optimizing for area, power, and timing. The subsequent physical design stages, including placement and routing, focus on the spatial arrangement of the logic gates and the interconnections between them, respectively, to form the final layout. Throughout these stages, sophisticated algorithms and tools are employed to ensure that the design meets the specified performance criteria while adhering to manufacturing constraints. The integration of ML techniques into each of these EDA stages is increasingly providing new opportunities for automation, optimization, and enhanced design quality [11]. Figure 2 illustrates typical ML methodologies applicable to different EDA stages, which is extended from [12]. Great success has been achieved by applying appropriate ML methods to design stages and corresponding data, such as CNN for placement optimization [13], GNN for netlist representation learning [14], and CNN+GNN for timing prediction [15]. LLMs would be depicted as supporting tools that interact with the human designers and engineers, providing assistance in areas where natural language understanding and generation are beneficial. Extended from [12]. improve the efficiency and effectiveness of the EDA process by automating routine tasks, enhancing decision-making, and facilitating better communication between the design teams and the EDA tools. 2.2 LLMs LLMs represent a significant advancement in the field of natural language processing (NLP) and have become a cornerstone of modern artificial intelligence. These models are characterized by their massive scale, often containing billions or even trillions of parameters, and their ability to generate coherent, contextually relevant, and human-like text. The core innovation that has enabled this leap forward is the Transformer architecture [16]. Transformers rely on self-attention mechanisms, which allow the model to weigh the importance of different words in a sentence, thereby capturing long-range dependencies and complex contextual relationships more effectively than previous architectures. It is observed that language model log-likelihood loss scales consistently as a power-law with model size, dataset size, and the amount of compute used for training [17], which is known as the scaling law of LLMs. Scaling up language models has shown to unpredictably bring about their emergent abilities [18], which are not present in smaller models but is present in larger models. Architectural Variants. Two primary architectural variants of transformers are commonly used in LLMs: encoder-only and decoder-only. Encoder-only models, such as BERT (i.e., Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Trans- formers) [19], consist solely of the encoder part of the original transformer architecture. They are designed for tasks that require understanding the input sequence, such as text classification, named entity recognition, and QA. These models are trained bidirectionally, meaning they can consider context from both the left and right sides of a token. A common pre-training task for encoder-only models is masked language modeling (MLM), where some tokens in the input are masked, and the model is trained to predict the original values of those tokens based on the surrounding context. On the other hand, decoder-only models, such as GPT-4 (i.e., Generative Pre-trained Trans- former) [1], use only the decoder part of the transformer architecture. They are well-suited for generative tasks, such as text completion, story writing, and code synthesis. These models are trained unidirectionally, predicting each token in a sequence based on the preceding tokens. This autoregressive nature makes them powerful for generating coherent and contextually relevant text. A typical pre-training task for decoder-only models is causal language modeling (CLM), where the model is trained to predict the next token in a sequence given the previous tokens. Wang et al. text: Large Language Models for EDA: Future or Mirage? 90:5 [20] have presented a large-scale evaluation of modeling choices and their impact on zero-shot generalization. Training Methods. Training LLMs involves several sophisticated techniques to ensure that the models can effectively learn from large datasets and generalize to a wide range of tasks. The process typically begins with pre-training, which is the initial phase where the model learns generalizable representations of language from a large corpus of text data. For encoder-only models, this often involves MLM, while for decoder-only models, it includes CLM. Given a sequence of tokens 𝑥 = {𝑥1, . . . ,𝑥𝑛}, the CLM task aims to autoregressively predict the target tokens 𝑥𝑖 based on the preceding tokens 𝑥<𝑖 in a sequence. A general training objective is to maximize the following likelihood: L𝐶𝐿𝑀 (𝑥) = 𝑛 ∑︁ 𝑖=1 log 𝑃(𝑥𝑖 | x<𝑖). (1) The goal of pre-training is to equip the model with a broad understanding of language that can be fine-tuned for specific tasks. After pre-training, the model undergoes supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which adapts the pre- trained model to perform well on particular NLP tasks. During SFT, the model is trained on a smaller, task-specific dataset, allowing it to specialize in the target application. This phase is crucial for tailoring the model’s capabilities to the specific requirements of the task, such as sentiment analysis, machine translation, or code generation. Finally, alignment is a critical step in ensuring that the model’s outputs are not only accurate but also aligned with human preferences and ethical standards. Alignment training aims to guide the model to produce responses that are safe, useful, and reflective of human values. Techniques such as reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) [21] and supervised alignment, where the model is trained on a dataset of human-generated examples, are employed. Alternative optimization techniques like direct preference optimization (DPO) [22] are proposed. Alignment ensures that the model generates high-quality, contextually appropriate, and ethically sound content. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) aims to reduce the number of trainable parameters while retaining a good performance as possible. LoRA [23] and its quantized counterpart QLoRA [24] are widely adopted Low-Rank Adaptation techniques, which freeze the pretrained model weights and inject trainable rank decomposition matrices into each layer of the Transformer architecture. The reparametrization can be described as ℎ =𝑊0𝑥 + Δ𝑊𝑥 =𝑊0𝑥 + 𝐵𝐴𝑥, (2) where 𝑊0 is the pretrained weight matrix, 𝐵 ∈ R𝑑×𝑟 , 𝐴 ∈ R𝑟 ×𝑘, and 𝑟 ≪ min (𝑑,𝑘). 2.3 LLM Augmentation Augmenting LLMs involves enhancing their capabilities through various techniques so that the model’s performance, adaptability, and ability to handle complex tasks are improved. Below, we describe some of these augmentation techniques, including chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and tooling agents. CoT Prompting. CoT Prompting [25] has gained significant attention due to its effectiveness in improving the reasoning abilities of LLMs. CoT prompting involves providing the model with a series of thought processes or logical steps that lead to a solution, rather than just presenting it with a problem and expecting an immediate answer. This method helps the model to develop a more structured and coherent way of thinking, allowing it to tackle complex questions that require multi-step reasoning, such as complex arithmetic, logical puzzles, and commonsense reasoning. RAG [27] combines the strengths of retrieval-based systems, which are adept at finding relevant information from a large corpus, with the generative capabilities of LLMs. In this framework, the model first retrieves relevant documents or pieces of information from a database and then uses this retrieved context to inform and improve the quality of the generated output. The integration of external knowledge not only enriches the content produced by the LLM but also ensures that the information is up-to-date and factually accurate, as the model can rely on a constantly updated source of information rather than being limited to its pre-training data. This dual mechanism of retrieval and generation makes RAG a powerful tool for tasks requiring both broad knowledge and precise detail. Figure 3(c) illustrates RAG workflow. Tooling Agents. Tooling agents [30] represent a sophisticated approach to augmenting the capabil- ities of LLMs by equipping them with access to external tools and services, such as APIs, databases, and specialized software, to gather, process, and utilize information. This integration allows LLMs to perform tasks that go beyond their inherent knowledge and computational limitations, thereby expanding their functionality and utility in real-world applications. The architecture of a tooling agent typically includes the LLM core, which is the pre-trained language model responsible for generating text and understanding natural language, and a tool interface layer, which acts as a middleware to facilitate communication between the LLM and the external tools. This layer handles API calls, data retrieval, and response formatting. Figure 3(d) illustrates examples of tooling agents. 3 Code Generation Code generation is a critical component of EDA, encompassing the automated creation of design artifacts such as HDL code, flow scripts, HLS outputs, and analog circuit descriptions. The applica- tion of LLMs to code generation offers significant opportunities to streamline these processes by automating repetitive tasks, generating complex code structures, and improving design efficiency. LLMs have the potential to translate high-level design specifications into HDL code, automate the creation of flow scripts for design and verification processes, generate HLS outputs from abstract functional descriptions, and even assist in analog circuit generation by producing parameterized templates. By leveraging their extensive training on diverse datasets, LLMs can reduce develop- ment time, improve accuracy, and enable the exploration of new design paradigms. This section provides a detailed analysis of the role of LLMs in code generation, their current capabilities, and the challenges and opportunities associated with their adoption in EDA workflows. 3.1 HDL Generation LLM-driven HDL generation leverages the sophisticated understanding and generative capabilities of these models to translate high-level design specifications into detailed RTL code, the foundational layer in digital circuit design. This process begins with the input of functional requirements or behavioral descriptions, often articulated in natural language or pseudo-code, which the LLM deciphers with unparalleled precision. The model then synthesizes this information, applying its deep knowledge of hardware design principles and RTL syntax, to output syntactically correct and logically sound RTL code. Recent studies measure code functional correctness through the pass@k metric [7], where a problem is considered solved if any of the 𝑘 samples pass the unit tests. An unbiased estimation is given by pass@k := E problem " 1 − 𝑛−𝑐 𝑘  𝑛 𝑘  # , (3) where 𝑛 ≥ 𝑘 samples are generated per task, in which 𝑐 ≤ 𝑛 samples pass testing. DAVE [31] investigates “English to Verilog translation” by a pretrained language model GPT-2. It targets a template-based, random auto-marking dataset, which are straightforward for translation. DAVE returned the correct answer in 94.8% of all validation tests, while bearing limitations like it cannot generate signal names that are not described. Tharkur et al. [32] characterize the ability of LLMs to generate useful Verilog. They curate Verilog datasets comprising of open-source Verilog code in public GitHub repositories as well as Verilog textbooks, which are used to fine-tune five pre-trained LLMs for evaluation. They report that fine-tuning LLMs over a specific language clearly improves completion performance: pre-tuned LLMs produced completions that are functionally correct only 1.09% of the time, while this number increases to 27.0% after tuning. A more comprehensive analysis has been reported in Verigen [33]. Tomlinson et al. [34] explore designing a Spiking Neuron Array using LLM. Vitolo et al. [35] investigate designing a recurrent spiking neural network while also generating test benches. Both implementations are submitted for fabrication in the SkyWater 130 nm technology. Sun et al. The original design specification is also transformed into a specific information list, such as state- transition table for sequential logic and truth table for combinational logic. Experiments on VerilogEval show that the proposed method outperforms the GPT4 baseline in all Pass@k settings, with up to 14.7% in VerilogEval-human Pass@10. MEV-LLM [38] integrates multiple LLMs, each specifically fine-tuned with dataset of a different complexity level. A complexity classifier LLM first assesses design complexity from the description prompt, and then forwards the task to the selected expert. Experiments show that the new multi- expert approach improves Verilog code generations by up to 23.9% using pass@k metrics compared with previous state-of-the-arts. Authors of HDL-GPT [39] hypothesize that training data (HDL code) quality is the key to create models with exceptional performance. They propose a data augmentation approach using CoT prompting, pipelining task-specific steps, such as language identification, adding comments, and testbench generation. The final validation stage compiles the code samples through the full EDA flow to GDS generation. HDL-GPT2 (fine-tuned StarCoder2) delivered the highest performance on VerilogEval, with 60.6% at pass@1, 78.5% at pass@5, and 81.4% at pass@10 on human eval, and 67.0% for pass@1, 86.0% for pass@5, and 90.2% for pass@10 on machine eval. BetterV [40] is a Verilog generation framework that performs design optimization through controlled code-to-code transformations. It integrates LLMs with discriminative guidance, enabling the system to generate Verilog code optimized for specific tasks. During the code generation process, the discriminator weighs the likelihood of the next token (code piece) being generated, based on both the language model’s prediction and the conditional probability of the token conforming to the desired design characteristics. Figure 4 illustates the guidance from generative discriminator. The pass@1 on VerilogEval-machine and VerilogEval-human for BetterV outperforms GPT-4 by 8.1% and 2.6%, respectively. It also has 46.52% fewer nodes in a ‘synthesis node reduction’ task, and saves 22.45% in another ‘verification runtime reduction’ task. In CodeV [41], authors argue that LLMs excel in summarizing Verilog code rather than generating them. Therefore, they propose to collect high-quality real-world Verilog data from Github, and then annotate them with LLMs. They introduce a multi-level summarization method, guiding LLMs (with few-shot examples) in first producing detailed descriptions and then abstracting high-level summaries. CodeV-CodeQwen achieves 77.6% pass@1 on the VerilogEval- machine benchmark and 53.2% on the VerilogEval-human benchmark, outperforming GPT-4 and previous SOTA model BetterV, and also achieves a 93.1% syntax pass rate and 55.2% function pass rate on the RTLLM benchmark, outperforming previous SOTA model RTLCoder. Overall flow of multi-agent VerilogCoder [42]. VerilogCoder [42] explores the use of multiple AI agents for autonomous Verilog code completion. A customized task planner is introduced, which is based on Task and Circuit Relation Graph that captures step-by-step sub-tasks and related circuit information (signal transition, etc.). A set of Verilog tools, such as syntax checker and AST-based waveform tracing tool, are utilized to assist agents for code implementation. Figure 5 illustrates the overall flow of VerilogCoder. The proposed VerilogCoder achieve 94.2% pass rate on VerilogEval-Human v2, including syntax and functional correctness, and outperform one of the state-of-the-art methods by 33.9%, i.e., without an agent-based approach. HaVen [43] presents a specialized framework for Verilog code generation that mitigates halluci- nations and aligns LLM outputs with HDL engineering practices. HaVen addresses three categories of hallucinations—symbolic, knowledge, and logical—through a structured methodology. It incorpo- rates Symbolic Interpretation-based Chain-of-Thought (SI-CoT) to accurately translate inputs such as truth tables and state diagrams into natural language instructions, a knowledge-enhanced dataset (K-dataset) to improve adherence to digital design conventions and Verilog-specific at- tributes, and a logical-enhanced dataset (L-dataset) to strengthen logical reasoning and handling of corner cases. These techniques are integrated into the framework to fine-tune LLMs, significantly improving Verilog code generation performance. Experimental results on benchmarks like Verilo- gEval and RTLLM demonstrate up to a 6.7% increase in pass@1 and a 4.7% increase in pass@5, outperforming state-of-the-art models. Fang et al. [44] introduce the use of LLMs for data augmentation in MasterRTL, a presynthesis PPA estimation framework for RTL designs. In the LLM-based data augmentation strategy, they generate hierarchical RTL designs by decomposing high-level design requirements into submodules and creating scalable, synthesizable Verilog code. This iterative process involves automated error detection and correction using synthesis feedback, ensuring the generated designs meet functional and structural requirements. The LLM-based approach complements a graph-based data augmen- tation method, enhancing diversity and hierarchy in the synthesized RTL dataset. By leveraging LLMs, MasterRTL effectively addresses the scarcity of high-quality RTL designs, improving the training of ML models for accurate PPA predictions and enabling transferable modeling across various design stages and technology nodes. [45] propose a Chain-of-Descriptions (CoDes) scheme to enhance HDL generation performance by outlining structured intermediate descriptive steps. The process first formulates a plan that breaks down the task into manageable steps. Next, it refines LLM responses by removing unnecessary boilerplate text and ensures style consistency. Finally, the refined plan is integrated with the input prompt to generate the LLM’s response. The introduction of intermediate descriptive steps enhances Granite-based models for a 40% improvement in the Pass@1 metric on testbenches. AutoVCoder [46] introduces an RAG mechanism that retrieves examples and knowledge from a domain-specific database. The retriever is trained on contrastive sample pairs, where a positive sam- ple pair is formed when the addition of a document chunk enhances the output quality of an LLM for a given question. It shows a 0.5% and 2.2% improvement in functional correctness on the Eval- Machine and EvalHuman benchmarks compared with BetterV, and achieves an increase in syntactic and functional correctness of up to 3.4% on the RTLLM benchmark compared with RTLCoder. Nair et al. [47] discuss prompt design techniques for secure hardware generation in scenarios listed in Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE). Feedback-in-the-loop. Autochip [48] aims for a fully automated approach that removes the designer from the loop. It enhances Verilog designs by automatically identifying and rectifying compilation errors and functional bugs in multiple rounds of interaction with a baseline LLM. In particular, outputs from compilation and debug tools with testbench simulations are collected to prompt the LLM to refine its implementation. Autochip improves the success rate against functional testbenches by on average 24.2% w.r.t. baseline generation. ChipGPT [49] includes both machine and human feedback in the iterative chip design flow. A correction manager checks program correctness using compiler and simulator, followed by an auxiliary human feedback stage. Chang et al. also design a post LLM search approach [50] to accomodate a design space exploration (DSE) process. EDA tools are employed to evaluate the PPA of each HDL program enumerated in a defined search tree. It has an area reduction of 47% compared with the original ChatGPT solution. Origen [51] introduces a self-reflection loop that comprises a base LLM with two trained LoRA models: Gen LoRA and Fix LoRA. Gen LoRA is responsible for interpreting natural language instruc- tions and generating initial RTL code, which then undergoes compilation evaluation. If the code fails to pass evaluation, Fix LoRA analyzes the error messages and the erroneous code, proposes and implements fixes to address the identified issues, and the corrected code is re-evaluated. OriGen surpasses the previous best-performing LLM by 12.8% on the VerilogEval-Human benchmark and is comparable with GPT-4 Turbo, and surpasses GPT-4 by 19.9% in syntactic correctness on the VerilogFixEval benchmark. AIvril [52] interweaves verification with the generative process, utilizing an AutoReview module and an AutoDV module. A review agent examines compilation logs for errors and generates structured review prompts to assist code refinement. Until syntax errors are resolved, the verification workflow begins and outputs coverage reports and failed assertions. The Review Agent similarly identifies discrepancies and formulates comprehensive review prompts. AIvril improves 1.32× and 2× in code quality on the VerilogEval-Human benchmark compared to CodeV and RTLFixer, respectively. VeriAssist [53] generates a test bench with test cases alongside the RTL code, which enables self-verification by analyzing code behavior considering time constraints. It then performs self- correction by identifying and rectifying compilation errors and functional bugs given feedback from the simulator. VeriAssist improves 7.5% and 7.0% pass@1 scores on VerilogEval-Machine and VerilogEval-Human, and improves 10.4% on the functionality pass@5 score on RTLLM with a syntax pass rate of 100% using GPT-4. text: Large Language Models for EDA: Future or Mirage? 90:11 VeriPPA [54] includes a dual-stage refinement protocol in the Verilog generation loop. The first stage leverages detailed error diagnostics from the simulator to rectify and evolve the Verilog code. The second stage further inspects PPA of the design by calling a commercial tool for logic synthesis. The design passes the PPA check if if is synthesizable and meets the PPA goal. Otherwise, both the design and its corresponding PPA report will be fed back to the LLM for refinement. VeriPPA achieves 62.0% (+16%) for functional accuracy and 81.37% (+8.3%) for syntactic correctness in Verilog code generation, compared to few-shot GPT4. RTLSquad [55] is an LLM-based multi-agent system designed for interpretable RTL code genera- tion and optimization. RTLSquad addresses the lack of decision interpretability in existing methods by dividing the design process into three stages: exploration, implementation, and verification and evaluation, each managed by specialized agent squads. Through collaborative communication and natural language exchanges, RTLSquad generates functionally correct RTL code, optimizes PPA (power, performance, and area) metrics, and provides detailed decision paths to justify design choices. Experiments conducted on the RTLLM dataset demonstrate that RTLSquad improves Pass@1 scores by up to 7.2% compared to baseline methods and achieves PPA metrics that match or exceed reference designs in 73.3% of cases. Hierarchy. Nakkab et al. [56] introduce hierarchical prompting that facilitates step-wise design methodology. The source of architectural hierarchy may come from either human-driven planning (HDHP) or purely automated generation (PGHP). Either way requires a hierarchy extraction step at the beginning to list all submodules necessary for design implementation. Then, the list is iterated over and LLM is responsible for producing HDL for each submodule. Finally, LLM is requested to integrate all generated submodules into a top-level module. ChatCPU [57] is an agile CPU design and verification platform powered by fine-tuned large language models LLMs to automate the end-to-end hardware design process. ChatCPU introduces a processor description language (PDL) for standardized CPU design specifications by encapsulating timing, functionality, pipeline architecture, and pin-to-pin interfaces, enabling automated HDL generation and the creation of a cycle-accurate reference model. Additionally, it in- corporates a module-interchangeable verification paradigm (MVP), which uses co-simulation between modularized RTL designs and golden reference models to verify functionality at both module and system levels. Leveraging fine-tuned LLMs, ChatCPU was used to design Saber6, a 6-stage in-order RISC-V CPU with 80,000 gates, successfully taped out using the SkyWater 130 nm MPW project. The platform achieved significant efficiency gains, including up to 12× acceleration in RTL coding, 9.33× in verification, and an average 3.81× reduction in design iteration time. HiVeGen [58] introduces a hierarchical LLM-based Verilog generation framework designed to address challenges in scalable and complex chip design, particularly for Domain-Specific Accelerators (DSAs). HiVeGen overcomes the limitations of traditional LLM-generated monolithic HDL code—such as token limits, code redundancy, and high error-correction costs—by decomposing designs into manageable hierarchical submodules. The framework integrates a Hierarchy-Aware Prompt Generation Engine for DSE and hierarchical decomposition, a Weight-Based Retrieving Engine to enhance module reuse and reduce redundant code generation, and an On-the-Fly Parsing Engine for real-time code feedback and error correction. HiVeGen also supports PPA-aware (Power, Performance, Area) optimization through ICL templates, enabling the generation of high-quality, reusable, and efficient designs. Experimental results demonstrate up to 30.97% token savings, 45.24% runtime reduction, and improved generation accuracy compared to existing methods, while successfully generating PPA-optimized DSA designs such as Systolic Arrays, CGRAs, and ShiDianNao accelerators.
