[59] formulate Verilog program generation as an RL problem, where the rewards are defined by calculating the similarity between the AST of the response and the AST of the ground truth code. The authors argue that auto-regressive training is not inherently aligned with the parallel semantics of Verilog code, and that a well-defined global supervisory signal is critical. It achieves syntax pass@5 of 93.1% and functional pass@5 of 55.2% on RTLLM. Search-based. Delorenzo et al. [60] present an automated transformer decoding algorithm that integrates Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). Specifically, in the MDP, the action is the vocabulary set of tokens of LLM, and the reward is determined based on the syntactical correctness, functional correctness, and PPA metric (the inverse area-delay product, larger the better) of the design. Comment line tokens are pruned to reduce the search space. Module reuse is also enabled so that LLMs can reference the generated sub-modules in their large-module generation, providing a more feasible MCTS iteration time. The MCTS technique can achieve a 31.8% improvement in the area-delay product for a 16-bit adder design generated by VeriGen. Multi-modality. Chang et al. [61] present a multi-modal generative model tailored for Verilog synthesis from visual-linguistic inputs. They argue that natural language is insufficient for accurately conveying the nested spatial structures of hardware as well as multi-module hardware design. Therefore, a multi-modal (figure+language) solution is proposed, which reduces token cost while enhancing the quality of the generated code. A hierarchical benchmark and related infrastructure captured in a query language, named VLMQL, are also proposed. With the integration of visual inputs, both syntax correctness and functionality correctness are greatly improved. Benchmark and Dataset. VerilogEval [62] is a benchmarking framework designed to evaluate the performance of Verilog code generation for hardware design and verification. The framework comprises a comprehensive evaluation dataset made up of 156 problems sourced from the Verilog instructional website HDLBits, covering a range from simple combinational circuits to complex finite state machines. Pinckey et al. [66] extend VerilogEval to support specification-to-RTL tasks in addition to the original code completion task. They also incorporate ICL prompts and a failure classification mechanism into the dataset, which allows for prompt engineering and failure analysis. VHDL-Eval [67] translates the programs in VerilogEval into VHDL, and enriches the dataset with publicly available VHDL problem sets from tutorials. Self-verifying testbenches are handcrafted for all the problems, adhering to the template of the VUnit Testing framework. RTLLM [63] proposes a comprehensive open-source benchmark dedicated to the automatic design RTL generation with natural languages. They summarize three progressive goals of the task, namely syntax goal (correctly synthesizable), functionality goal (passing test cases), and quality goal (good PPA). RTLLM has collected 30 common designs, including 11 arithmetic designs and 19 logic designs. Each design in the benchmark consists of a natural language description of design functionality, a testbench, and a hand-crafted Verilog implementation. OpenLLM-RTL [68] introduces the updated RTLLM 2.0, which is augmented to 50 hand-crafted designs. RTL-Repo [74] is a benchmark for Verilog code completion. Verilog repositories are collected via Github API, and random, nonempty, non-comment lines of code are randomly selected to be the target line for model prediction. RTL-Repo contains 4,098 samples, ranging from 2K to 128K tokens, and each sample contains the context of the entire repository, the code of the current file being edited, excluding the target line and all lines after it, and the target line itself. Exact Match and Edit Similarity are used as evaluation metrics for the benchmark. PyHDL-Eval [73] is a framework for evaluating LLMs on specification-to-RTL tasks in the context of Python-embedded domain specific languages (DSLs). It includes 168 problems, each containing Verilog reference solutions, Verilog test benches, Python test scripts, and workflow orchestration ACM Trans. Des. Autom. Electron. Authors of RTLCoder [64] have introduced a training dataset generation flow composed of three stages: RTL domain keywords preparation, instruction generation, and reference code generation. In the first stage, commonly used logic components ( adder, FSM, etc.) are generated by traversing a category tree, forming a keyword pool. Then, keywords are sampled and fed to GPT for instruction generation, namely to generate a specific design description for the target component. Finally, implementation code is automatically generated by prompting GPT. By going through all three stages and extra validation procedures, a total of 27, 000 data samples are generated in their work for model training. OpenLLM-RTL [68] introduces the extended RTLCoder-data dataset of 80K instruction-code data samples. MG-Verilog [72] is a multi-grained Verilog dataset that encompasses descriptions at various levels of detail and corresponding code samples. The dataset consists of over 11, 000 Verilog code samples, each with natural language descriptions ranging from high-level summaries to detailed, line-by-line comments. Goh et al. [71] have published a labelled Verilog dataset of 68, 122 data entries, where each entry contains a single module, followed by an LLM-generated description of the module. Authors of AI-HDLCoder [70] release an AI-HDLCoder-Dataset with over 100,000 rows of VHDL code, which are mainly collected from online sources and deduplicated using Jaccard similarity and Min-Hash techniques. SA-DS [75] is a systolic array-based accelerator dataset comprising spatial array designs fol- lowing the standardized Berkeley’s Gemmini accelerator generator template. Each data point in SA-DS includes a natural language description of the accelerator’s micro-architecture and a Chisel description, facilitating LLM-based hardware accelerator design by few-shot learning. Fu et al. [69] propose to utilize version control data from hardware projects to construct semi- synthetic dataset. The reason is that version control serves as a database that captures snapshots of a project at any given moment and offers a precise explanation of the project’s evolution. The 5W1H (Who, What, When, Where, Why, How) journalistic principles serve as a framework to describe the modification of code. In CraftRTL [65], Liu et al. present an analysis of fine-tuned LLMs on synthetic data. They report that models underperform on problems involving non-textual input formats, such as K-map and waveforms. Therefore, a correct-by-construction solution is proposed to deal with non-textual representations. To mitigate “minor” errors produced by LLMs, they also construct a debug dataset by injecting identified errors into correct code snippets. MetRex [76] introduces a dataset for evaluating the ability of LLMs to reason about post-synthesis metrics of Verilog HDL designs, such as area, delay, and static power. The MetRex dataset comprises 25, 868 Verilog designs annotated with their corresponding post-synthesis metrics, alongside a CoT prompting template to improve LLM reasoning by breaking down metric estimation into logical steps. The authors demonstrate that supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on MetRex significantly improves the accuracy of LLM-based metric estimation, with gains of 37.0%, 25.3%, and 25.7% for area, delay, and static power, respectively, compared to few-shot prompting techniques. Compared to traditional regression-based methods, the fine-tuned LLM achieves 17.4% higher accuracy within a 5% error margin and 1.7× faster runtime by eliminating preprocessing overheads. While LLMs show promise for metric reasoning in smaller designs, challenges remain for complex designs and advanced metrics like dynamic power. text: Large Language Models for EDA: Future or Mirage? 90:15 FormalEval [78] introduces a formal evaluation method designed to automatically assess the functional correctness of code generated by LLMs without the need for manual test case creation. It utilizes a Sequential Equivalence Checking (SEC) engine, which is capable of automatically and comprehensively checking whether the implemented code behaves identically to the specified one across all possible input scenarios. If the two programs are functionally equivalent, FormalEval returns a “Proven” statement; if not, it provides a “Falsified” statement along with a counterexample, which is an input that causes a behavioral discrepancy. Additionally, the authors propose two approaches to integrate FormalEval with LLM training: an explicit neural network-based functional checking proxy and an implicit functionality loss signal during the learning process. They reported a 23% evaluation error in existing RTL benchmarking dataset by using their method. SimEval [79] introduces a comprehensive multifaceted metric designed to assess the similarity of HDL codes generated by LLMs. The metric evaluates similarity at three levels: syntactic (using abstract syntax trees), semantic (based on control flow graphs), and functional/structural (via synthesized gate-level netlists). SimEval leverages techniques such as Jaccard similarity for AST analysis, graph kernels for CFG comparison, and shortest path kernels for netlist evaluation. The authors applied SimEval to assess dataset diversity in RTL codes generated by state-of-the-art LLM-based frameworks like RTLCoder, revealing significant issues with diversity across clusters of generated designs. Watermarking. RTLMarker [80] discusses hardware watermarking that protects RTL code gener- ated by LLMs. It employs a rule-based Verilog code transformation set that ensures the functional correctness of watermarked code while embedding robust and transparent watermarks into both the RTL code and the synthesized gate-level netlist. The framework includes three core modules: a watermark embedding module, a feature representation module, and a watermark detection module, with joint optimization to balance transparency and effectiveness. Evaluations on benchmarks like RTLLM and VerilogEval show that RTLMarker achieves over 95% accuracy at the RTL level and demonstrates resilience against variable name replacement attacks. 3.2 System-level Design System-level design represents a high-level abstraction in the hardware development process, focusing on functional modeling, architectural exploration, and design space tradeoffs rather than direct RTL implementation. Unlike traditional HDL code generation, which emphasizes the precise, low-level implementation of hardware modules, system-level design deals with algorithm-to- hardware translation, hardware-software partitioning, and macro-level decisions, such as selecting appropriate architectures or optimizing communication protocols. The key challenge in LLM-driven system-level design lies in bridging the gap between functional specifications and synthesizable hardware descriptions while ensuring PPA tradeoffs are considered. Yan et al. [81] propose a novel framework, LLM-based Co-Design Accelerator (LCDA), that LLMs to address the “cold start” problem in software-hardware (SW-HW) co-design for deep neural networks (DNNs). LCDA uses pre-trained LLMs, specifically GPT-4, as design optimizers, allowing the framework to utilize heuristic knowledge from prior research and bypass the random initialization typically required in RL or genetic algorithm methods. The framework co-designs DNN topologies and Compute-in-Memory (CiM) DNN accelerators, achieving a 25× speedup compared to the state-of-the-art NACIM method while maintaining comparable performance. In GPT4AIGChip [82], authors investigate the limitations and capabilities of leveraging existing LLMs to generate AI accelerator designs. After analyzing their common failures, they propose an LLM-friendly hardware design template, emphasizing high modularity, decoupled module design, and deep design hierarchies to facilitate step-by-step design generation. The article demonstrates AiEDA’s capabilities through the design of a low-power digital ASIC for Keyword Spotting (KWS), showcasing hardware optimization strategies for power, area, and accuracy tradeoffs. Salcedo et al. [87] introduce leveraging Generative AI, specifically GPT-4, to design and verify a vector processor SoC using open-source tools. The authors developed the SoC, including all SystemVerilog hardware blocks, C firmware, and test cases, through GPT-4, employing iterative prompt engineering and refinement techniques. The design incorporates a vector coprocessor integrated with an RISC-V CPU via the Wishbone bus and supports vector instructions for integer, bitwise, scalar, and floating-point operations. A hierarchical, iterative design process was used, combining GPT-4-generated code with human validation and functional testing via PyMTL3. The SoC was fabricated using the OpenLane flow and Sky130 PDK, achieving a 1.32𝑚𝑚2 area and 231 mW power consumption. Key contributions include insights into effective GPT-4 prompting strategies, such as generate-and-merge and example-based prompting, to address challenges like context window limits and complex module generation. 3.3 Flow Script Generation Flow script generation represents a critical aspect that significantly impacts the efficiency and automation of the entire design process. Flow scripts, which are essential for orchestrating the sequence of operations within EDA tools, dictate the steps from synthesis to place-and-route, simulation, and verification. Traditionally, these scripts have been crafted manually, requiring deep expertise and a meticulous understanding of the toolchain. However, with the advent of LLMs, there is now an opportunity to automate the creation of these complex and often repetitive scripts. LLMs can interpret high-level design requirements and generate corresponding flow scripts that are not only syntactically correct but also optimized for specific design goals. This capability not only reduces the time and effort required for script writing but also minimizes the potential for human error, leading to more reliable and efficient design flows. By integrating LLM-driven flow script generation into the EDA workflow, designers can focus on higher-level tasks, such as architecture exploration and performance optimization, thereby accelerating the development cycle and improving overall productivity. ChatEDA [88] is an innovative framework that leverages a LLM to automate the EDA process. The primary objective of ChatEDA is to interpret natural language commands and generate executable scripts that can be used to drive EDA tools, thereby streamlining the design flow from RTL to Graphic Data System Version II (GDSII). ChatEDA is designed as an autonomous agent that can understand and respond to user requirements in natural language. It breaks down complex tasks into smaller, manageable sub-tasks and generates Python scripts to execute these tasks using EDA tools. At the core of ChatEDA is AutoMage, a fine-tuned LLM specifically adapted for EDA tasks. AutoMage is trained to understand and generate code that interacts with EDA tools, such as OpenROAD, through their APIs. The workflow consists of three main stages: task planning, script generation, and task execution. AutoMage interprets the user’s natural language requirements, plans the necessary sub-tasks, and then generates the corresponding Python scripts. A comprehensive evaluation benchmark, ChatEDA-bench, is also developed, which comprises 50 distinct tasks spanning three distinct categories: simple flow calls, complex flow calls, and parameter flow calls. Unlike traditional methods that involve manually writing HLS code, the integration of LLMs enables automated generation of synthesizable HLS code from functional descriptions, design requirements, or even natural language inputs. LLMs can assist in creating HLS code that incorporates proper hardware constructs, such as pipelining, loop unrolling, and parallelism, while ensuring the code is compliant with synthesis guidelines. By leveraging their ability to analyze and learn from large datasets of HLS examples, LLMs can not only generate code but also provide suggestions for op- timization and best practices, drastically reducing development time and improving design quality. The process is broken down into small steps to allow the LLM to transform the original C into synthesizable C, such as removing print statements, optimizing data types using arbitrary width integers, and so on. Xu et al. [94] similarly target an LLM-driven program repair framework that takes regular C/C++ code as input and automatically generates its corresponding HLS-C code for synthesis. A repair library containing correction templates for HLS is manually established. HLS-incompatible errors, such as the unsupported “pointer-to-pointer” feature, are identified and fixed with RAG-guided tem- plates. The proposed LLM-driven repair framework can achieve much higher repair pass rates on 24 real-world applications compared with the traditional scripts and the direct applications of the LLM. HLSPilot [95] is a framework that leverages LLMs to automate the generation and optimization of HLS code for hybrid CPU-FPGA architectures. The methodology begins with runtime profiling to identify performance bottlenecks in sequential C/C++ code. HLSPilot then extracts and optimizes these critical code segments using LLMs, which are guided by ICL and a set of predefined C-to- HLS optimization strategies. The optimized HLS code is further refined through DSE for pragma parameter tuning, and the final step involves offloading the compute kernels to the FPGA using Xilinx OpenCL APIs. This approach aims to bridge the semantic gap between high-level software and hardware design, enabling more efficient and automated hardware acceleration. In a case study involving the L-BFGS algorithm, HLSPilot achieved over 11 times speedup in runtime on a hybrid CPU-FPGA platform. Swaroopa et al. [96] discuss LLM-based automatic generation of annotated C++ code suitable for HLS. They find that LLMs could not correctly deal with the K-maps problems. Meech [97] case studies designing a Random Number Generator using Amaranth Python scripts. Liao et al. [98] survey recent work in LLM for HLS, and they call for attention to power/energy implications in current research. The LLM solution reduces resource utilization for 38.67%, improves execution cycles for 64%, and reduces power consumption for 38.67%. For the critical path, the HLS-based approach outperformed LLM-based approaches by 28.82%. SynthAI [99] is a multi-agent generative AI framework designed for the automated generation of modular HLS designs. SynthAI leverages advanced LLM technologies, including ReAct agents, CoT prompting, and RAG, integrated within a structured decision graph to decompose complex hardware design tasks into smaller, manageable modules. The framework includes agents for system design, module design, evaluation, and integration, which iteratively generate synthesizable HLS code, test benches, and header files while adhering to user-defined goals and requirements. SynthAI utilizes real-time web searches, database queries, and Python execution to enhance its design capabilities. Case studies, including the design of a 128-point FFT circuit, a quadruple-precision floating-point exponentiation module, and a simple RISC-V CPU, demonstrate SynthAI’s proficiency in generating modular, synthesizable, and optimized HLS designs. ChatChisel [100] explores generating Chisel code for RTL-level circuit design. Four LLM modules are utilized for design decomposition, Chisel code generation, tool-enhanced correction (i.e., debug), and top-level module composition, respectively. A five-stage RISC-V RV32I CPU has been designed using the ChatChisel workflow. Gai et al. [101] examine the use of LLMs to automate hardware design generation through HLS. The authors address challenges such as limited HDL training data, semantic misalignment between pre-trained LLMs and HDLs, and the high token cost of HDL generation by leveraging HLS, which shares syntax and semantics with programming languages like C/C++. They introduce a dataset of over 42, 000 HLS programs and fine-tune pre-trained models (e.g., Code-Llama) for HLS design generation, utilizing techniques like CoT prompting and feedback loops for iterative improvements. Results show gains in syntax correctness (from 54.85% to 94.33%) and functional correctness (from 0% to 61.45%), with generated HLS designs achieving reasonable performance on FPGA hardware. text: 90:20 Z. He et al. 3.5 Analog Design Generation The integration of LLMs into EDA has opened new horizons for automating circuit design through advanced code generation techniques. Unlike digital design, which benefits from standardized components like logic gates and well-defined abstraction layers, analog design inherently deals with continuous signal processing, non-linear behaviors, and highly sensitive performance requirements. In analog circuits, even small changes in component values or topologies can result in significant variations in performance metrics, such as gain, bandwidth, or power consumption. This makes analog design less amenable to traditional automation techniques, as it requires precise modeling of physical components (e.g., transistors, resistors, and capacitors) and their interactions in a real-world context. Furthermore, analog design often lacks the robust hierarchical abstraction layers seen in digital workflows, where higher-level functionality can often be decoupled from lower-level implementation details. Instead, analog design workflows require a tight integration between topology, parameter selection, and performance validation, which increases the complexity of automation. These complexities give rise to distinct subfields within analog design automation, each address- ing a specific stage of the design process. Specification-to-netlist translation focuses on converting high-level descriptions, often in natural language, into machine-readable circuit representations (e.g., SPICE netlists). Topology synthesis, on the other hand, explores or generates new circuit configurations, aiming to identify novel or optimized topologies that meet design objectives such as gain, noise, or power efficiency. Schematic-to-netlist and netlist-to-schematic transformations bridge the gap between human-readable graphical representations and machine-readable textual descriptions, enabling better integration between design, simulation, and debugging workflows. Fi- nally, layout generation translates circuit designs into detailed physical layouts that meet fabrication constraints, a process that requires careful attention to parasitics, design rule checking (DRC), and layout-versus-schematic (LVS) validation. Each of these categories presents unique challenges. For example, spec-to-netlist translation must ensure functional correctness while interpreting ambiguous or incomplete specifications. Topology synthesis faces the difficulty of navigating vast and complex design spaces, often requiring the exploration of millions of potential configurations. Schematic-to-netlist and netlist-to-schematic transformations must maintain consistency between representations while ensuring that the design intent is preserved. Layout generation requires not only the accurate placement and routing of components but also the optimization of performance metrics such as area, power, and signal integrity while adhering to manufacturing constraints. LLMs, with their ability to process and generate natural language, code, and structured data, have the potential to address these challenges by automating traditionally labor-intensive tasks and enabling faster design iterations. As progress continues, LLMs could serve as a critical tool for bridging the gap between high-level design intent and low-level implementation, transforming the historically manual and expertise-driven process of analog circuit design. Spec-to-Netlist. AnalogCoder [102] is a training-free LLM agent designed for analog circuit design through Python code generation. The methodology includes a feedback-enhanced flow with tailored domain-specific prompts, enabling automated and self-correcting design of analog circuits. The LLM generates Python code for the desired analog circuit functionalities, leveraging its strong Python programming capabilities. A circuit tool library archives successful designs as reusable modular sub- circuits, simplifying the creation of composite circuits. The feedback-enhanced design flow involves several stages, including requirement check, simulation and operating point check, DC sweep check, and function check, to ensure the correctness of the generated code. AnalogCoder outperforms existing LLM-based methods, such as GPT-4o, in solving circuit design tasks, successfully completing 20 out of 24 benchmark tasks, which include both basic and composite circuits. text: Large Language Models for EDA: Future or Mirage? 90:21 Atelier [103] is a novel framework leveraging general-purpose LLMs and a curated domain- specific knowledge base to automate analog circuit design. Addressing challenges of data scarcity and domain expertise requirements, Atelier employs multiple specialized LLM-based agents struc- tured in a Graph-of-Thoughts (GoT) architecture, with each agent responsible for specific design steps such as topology selection, circuit analysis, parameter tuning, topology modification, and design decision-making. The framework integrates advanced techniques like RAG, CoT reasoning, self-reflection, backtracking, and external tools (e.g., CMA-ES optimizer) to enhance interpretability and design efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate Atelier’s superiority over black-box opti- mization methods, general-purpose LLMs, and state-of-the-art LLM-based methods like Artisan, achieving higher success rates, superior performance metrics, and reduced runtimes across diverse opamp design tasks. SPICECopilot [104] introduces a framework designed to automate SPICE code generation and simulation using LLMs and the PySpice Python library. SPICEPilot addresses the limitations of existing LLMs in hardware-specific tasks, such as inaccurate gate width/length ratios, improper input signals, and incorrect circuit analysis. The framework generates SPICE code through prompt engineering, validates it using automated feedback loops, and creates a comprehensive open-source dataset to mitigate data scarcity in analog circuit design. It also introduces benchmarking metrics for evaluating LLM performance across various circuit complexities and demonstrates superior results compared to existing analog circuit generation benchmarks. PICBench [105] introduces the first comprehensive open-source benchmarking framework de- signed to evaluate the capabilities of LLMs in automating Photonic Integrated Circuits (PICs) design. PICBench includes 24 meticulously crafted design problems, spanning optical computing, optical interconnects, optical switches, and fundamental devices, with varying complexities and scales. The framework enables automatic evaluation of LLM-generated PIC netlists through syn- tax validation and functionality testing using the open-source simulator SAX. A feedback-based prompt engineering method is proposed to iteratively refine designs, addressing common syntax and functional errors, thus enhancing model performance. The study evaluates state-of-the-art LLMs, such as GPT-4 and Gemini 1.5 Pro, demonstrating the impact of feedback mechanisms and restrictions in improving syntax and functionality correctness. Topology Synthesis. Artisan [106] is an automated operational amplifier (opamp) design frame- work that leverages a domain-specific LLM to integrate knowledge-driven reasoning with code generation for analog circuits. It introduces a bidirectional circuit representation that aligns netlists with natural language descriptions, enabling semantic understanding of circuit topology and func- tionality. Using Tree-of-Thoughts (ToT) and CoTs methodologies, Artisan models the hierarchical opamp design process as a multi-agent QA sequence, facilitating tasks like topology selection, parameter tuning, and performance optimization. Artisan generates behavioral and transistor-level netlists, automating the analog design process while offering interpretability and efficiency. Ex- perimental results demonstrate that Artisan outperforms state-of-the-art black-box optimization methods (e.g., Bayesian and RL approaches) and general-purpose LLMs by achieving higher success rates, competitive circuit performance, and up to 50.1× faster design cycles. LaMAGIC [107] leverages supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of LLMs for automated topology generation of analog circuits, specifically power converters. The framework enables direct one- shot generation of optimized circuit designs from user-defined specifications, overcoming the inefficiencies of traditional manual design and simulation-intensive search methodologies like RL. LaMAGIC introduces and evaluates multiple innovative circuit formulations, including canonical, adjacency-matrix-based, and float-input-based representations, to address challenges in represent- ing analog circuits as graphs and ensure compatibility with the autoregressive nature of LLMs. ACM Trans. Schemetic-to-Netlist. Auto-SPICE [108] is a fully automated framework that leverages LLMs and computer vision techniques to generate SPICE netlists—a textual representation of analog circuits— from schematic images. The framework addresses key challenges in component recognition, net connectivity, and netlist verification by combining object detection (e.g., YOLO for component detection), deep Hough transform for net detection, and prompt tuning for LLMs like GPT-4. Auto-SPICE builds a pipeline to extract SPICE netlists directly from analog circuit diagrams in textbooks and research papers, reducing the need for manual annotations. The framework also includes a feedback-based netlist verification mechanism to improve accuracy. Using Auto-SPICE, the authors created a dataset of 2,100 SPICE netlists, which was used to fine-tune GPT-4-mini for improved netlist generation from circuit descriptions. Experimental results show that Auto-SPICE outperforms prior methods (e.g., AMSNet) in accuracy and scalability, achieving 100% structural similarity in generated netlists. Netlist-to-Schemetic. Schemato [109] introduces a fine-tuned LLM designed to convert cir- cuit netlists into human-readable schematics in two formats: LTSpice-compatible .asc files and CircuitTikZ-based LaTeX code for visualizing schematics. Schemato leverages supervised instruc- tion tuning and data augmentation on a curated dataset of netlist-to-schematic pairs, enabling it to outperform state-of-the-art models, including GPT-4o and Llama-3.1-8B, across multiple evaluation metrics. It achieves a compilation success rate (CSR) of up to 93.75% for the netlist-to-LATEX task and generates schematics with a mean structural similarity index measure (MSSIM) three times higher than baseline models. Unlike heuristic-based approaches, Schemato generalizes across circuit types without requiring predefined templates or aesthetic rules by learning from human-designed examples. While demonstrating high accuracy for simpler circuits, the model struggles with larger, more complex topologies, highlighting the need for larger and more diverse training datasets. Layout Generation. LayoutCopilot [110] is an interactive analog layout design framework powered by multi-agent collaboration. It accepts both high-level design intents and concrete requests in natural language from designers and then transforms them into precise executable commands. Concrete requests are directly handled by a concrete request processor that decomposes concrete tasks into subtasks corresponding to layout tool commands. For abstract requests, high-level suggestions are generated, which are transformed to concrete requests if they are accepted by the designer. The GLayout framework [111] translates analog layout into a compact, technology-generic text representation. It fine-tunes an LLM using RAG to understand this text representation and generate layouts based on new information provided in-context. The LLM is trained on a dataset of less than 50 unique circuits and text documents providing layout knowledge. The framework uses open-source LLMs with varying parameter sizes (3, 7, and 22 billion parameters) to handle tasks ranging from simple 2-transistor circuits to more complex ΔΣ ADCs. The LLM is capable of translating general human language prompts into analog layout, making the design process more intuitive and accessible. Hardware verification, which ensures that a design behaves as intended, is a time-consuming and resource-intensive process, often involving tasks such as writing SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA), developing simulation-based testbenches, and address- ing security vulnerabilities. LLMs have the potential to automate and enhance these critical aspects by leveraging their ability to interpret natural language specifications, learn from existing veri- fication patterns, and generate high-quality, synthesizable code. For SVA generation, LLMs can translate functional requirements into precise assertions to ensure critical properties hold through- out the design. In testbench generation, they can produce Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) components, test stimuli, and coverage models to rigorously validate hardware behavior. Additionally, LLMs can assist in identifying and mitigating security vulnerabilities, such as side- channel attacks or hardware Trojans, by analyzing design specifications and suggesting verification strategies. By streamlining these processes, LLMs offer the promise of reducing verification effort, improving coverage, and strengthening design security, making them an indispensable tool in modern hardware development. 4.1 Assertion Generation NL2SVA [116] translates the circuit under verification and the specifications in natural langauge into an array of intermediate representations, which contains candidate SVA. Sub-translation is also provided, which decomposes the requirement and maps formalization back to parts of the natural language. Designers can edit the sub-translation to incorporate human feedback. Hassan et al. [117] present a methodology that combines LLMs with formal verification and mutation testing to generate and evaluate invariants for hardware designs. The approach is divided into three stages: generating invariants from design specifications, creating a formal model from the Verilog behavioral model, and performing a qualitative analysis of the invariants using mutation testing. This method leverages LLMs to automate the generation of invariants and formal models, while mutation testing is employed to assess the quality and robustness of these invariants. Aditi et al. [118] introduce a method for automatically converting natural language specifications into validated SVAs using fine-tuned LLMs. The approach involves generating multiple candidate SVAs from the natural language specification, followed by a validation process that uses a second ACM Trans. Des. Autom. Electron. Syst., Vol. 30, No. 6, Article 90. Publication date: October 2025.

text: Large Language Models for EDA: Future or Mirage? 90:25 language model to convert the generated SVA back into an English statement. This English statement is then compared to the original specification to ensure syntactic and semantic compatibility, thereby validating the generated SVA. Experimental results show that 92% of the specs were correctly converted to the corresponding SVAs. AssertLLM [119] is an automatic assertion generation framework for complete specification files. The process is decomposed into three steps: information extraction, signal name mapping, and SVA generation. LLMs are guided to verify signal bitwidth, connectivity, and functionality. A benchmark that contains both golden specification documents and golden RTL designs is released. Figure 8(a) illustrates AssertLLM workflow. Evaluation on a full design with 23 I/O signals shows that 89% of the generated assertions are both syntactically and functionally accurate. ChIRRAG [121] is a framework that leverages LLMs to generate SVAs from natural language specifications of a design. It first transforms unstructured design specifications into a standardized JSON format. This structured input is then provided to the LLM, which generates an initial set of SVAs. The generated assertions are subsequently validated through simulation, and any errors, such as syntax or simulation failures, are identified. The LLM iteratively refines the assertions based on feedback from the simulation logs, ensuring that the final SVA suite is both syntactically and semantically correct. The process includes manual intervention when necessary, particularly for implementation bugs or issues that the LLM cannot resolve automatically. Only 27% of the generated SVA require refinement upon iterative prompting. LAAG-RV [122] presents a framework that also targets generating SVA from natural language specifications of RTL designs using LLM. It starts with preprocessing the RTL design files, dividing them into submodules, and extracting concise abstract descriptions that capture relevant design data such as I/O ports and functionality. These abstracts, along with the natural language specifications, are then fed into an LLM to generate initial SVA assertions. The generated assertions are validated through simulation, and any issues are iteratively refined by providing the LLM with carefully crafted manual prompts derived from simulation failures. This iterative process ensures that the final assertions are both syntactically and semantically correct, and a one-time Verilog loop is used to synchronize signal names, enhancing the quality of the generated SVAs. Orenes et al. [123] explore whether LLMs can generate SVA for a given design without any specification beyond the RTL. Human efforts are involved in the iterative generation process to ‘teach’ LLMs how to generate correct assertions. This is done by crafting a rule set in plain natural language based on expert knowledge of SVA, such as “&bitarray means that ALL the bits are ONES”. Their AutoSVA2 framework is able to generate correct SVA from buggy RTL, which improves coverage of RTL behavior by up to 6×, and has exposed a bug in the RISC-V CVA6 Ariane core. 4.2 Testbench Generation AutoBench [120] is an LLM-automated testbench generation and evaluation framework for hard- ware verification. Given RTL description and module header, AutoBench first generates an HDL implementation, which is used to discriminate the circuit type into CMB or SEQ. A Verilog driver track and a Python checker track are responsible for generating the test stimuli input and the expected output, respectively. AutoEval introduced in the same article is a system to assess the generated test benches with three criteria, including syntactic correctness, no error with golden RTL, and a mutant-based coverage-oriented evaluation. Figure 8(b) illustrates AutoBench workflow. Au- toBench demonstrates a 57% improvement in the testbench Eval2 pass@1 ratio, and 3.36 times Eval2 pass@1 ratio for sequential circuits. CorrectBench [124] is an extension of AutoBench, designed to overcome its key limitations in testbench generation for HDL design. While AutoBench relies solely on syntax self-checking and lacked functional validation and correction mechanisms, it leads to low success rates, particularly for sequential circuits. CorrectBench addresses these shortcomings by ACM Trans. Des. Autom. Electron. Syst., Vol. 30, No. 6, Article 90. Publication date: October 2025.

This extension enhances performance, achieving a 70.13% pass ratio compared to AutoBench’s 52.18%, and demonstrates a 66.18% improvement for sequential circuits. LLM4DV [125] presents a test stimuli generation framework. A coverage plan, i.e., a list of coverage points to be tested, is maintained and provided to the LLM at each iteration step, where LLM is requested for a test stimuli. Sampling techniques are utilized to handle the large number of uncovered bins. Bhandari et al. [126] discuss LLM-aided Testbench Generation for Finite-State Machines (FSMs). Given the specification and the design RTL of DUT, LLM is prompted to generate an initial testbench, which undergoes a compilation check using commercial tool. If any errors are detected during compilation, these errors are appended to the prompt and fed back to the LLM for refining the testbench. Next, the FSM is simulated in coverage analysis mode, where uncovered FSM transitions are reported and fed back to LLM to generate new test cases. LLM-TG [127] is a framework leveraging LLMs to automate and enhance processor test case generation for design verification. LLM-TG addresses challenges in traditional verification, such as the time-intensive and error-prone nature of manual test case creation, by employing a structured workflow comprising prompt-based test case construction, LLM-assisted optimization, test result feedback, and a reusable prompt library. The framework generates both inline assembly and C programs, improves test case correctness through iterative feedback, and boosts test efficiency by reusing validated prompts. Experiments on an RV64GC-based processor (Xuantie-C910) demon- strate that LLM-TG achieves 8.34% higher block coverage and 5.8% higher expression coverage compared to state-of-the-art methods like RISCV-DV and LLM4DV. Additionally, the prompt library reduces token consumption by over 50%, accelerating subsequent verification processes. VerilogReader [128] introduces a framework that integrates LLMs, into the Coverage Directed Test Generation (CDG) process for automatic hardware test generation. The framework positions LLMs as “VerilogReaders”, enabling them to comprehend Verilog code and generate test stimuli to maximize code coverage. Key innovations include the DUT Explainer, which provides natural language descriptions and test guidance for designs, and the Coverage Explainer, which reformats coverage reports into LLM-readable formats to assist in generating inputs for unexplored code branches. Evaluated on a benchmark suite of 24 Verilog designs, VerilogReader outperforms random testing, achieving full code coverage on simple and medium-level designs while highlighting LLM limitations with more complex circuits. The study also explores scalability challenges, showing a decline in performance with larger designs, and suggests future directions such as integrating LLMs with Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to improve structural comprehension and scalability for real-world hardware verification tasks. 4.3 Security DIVAS [129] identifies security vulnerabilities from user-defined SoC specifications. It first maps them to the relevant CWEs, followed by the generation of equivalent assertions. An extensive CWE database is constructed to help filter LLM response. Kande et al. [130] investigate the use of LLMs for hardware security assertion generation. To enable this, designer intents are captured in a comment string specifying the properties that are checked. Design source, example assertions, together with the comment strings, are organized into a prompt string to query the LLM. Out-of-the-box code LLMs are used to comprehensively evaluate the framework, achieving an accuracy of up to 93.55% across all the benchmarks, compared to the 26.54% average accuracy with all prompt configurations of varying levels of context. text: Large Language Models for EDA: Future or Mirage? 90:27 SPICED [131] introduces a framework designed to detect and localize syntactical bugs and analog Trojans in circuit netlists. The methodology employs CoT reasoning and few-shot examples to teach the LLM anomaly detection rules. Specifically, the LLM is provided with SPICE netlists and corresponding simulation log files, along with detailed circuit specifications. The LLM is trained to identify and flag syntactical bugs such as missing nodes, incorrect component definitions, and floating nodes, and to detect and locate Trojans by analyzing deviations in voltage and current behaviors. The process involves iteratively refining the LLM’s understanding of SPICE syntax and circuit behavior through feedback, ensuring that it can accurately pinpoint and describe the nature and location of detected anomalies. This approach leverages the LLM’s NLP capabilities to enhance the detection and localization of both syntactical bugs and Trojans without requiring explicit training or hardware modifications. It achieves an average Trojan coverage of 93.32% and an average true positive rate of 93.4% in identifying Trojan-impacted nodes for the evaluated analog benchmark circuits. LASP [132] (LLM Assisted Security Property Generation) is a framework designed to automate the generation of security properties for SoC verification. The methodology begins with preprocessing and decomposing the RTL design into sub-modules, extracting concise summaries that include module hierarchy, interfaces, and key design features. These summaries, along with the design specifications and a detailed threat model, are then provided to an LLM. The LLM generates natural language security properties based on this information. The process also involves a hybrid approach that combines static analysis to extract control and data flow features with LLM capabilities to identify additional security-critical features, ensuring comprehensive coverage of security assets. 80% of the generated properties were readily translatable into SVAs and tested using formal tools. Assert-O [133] extracts security properties from hardware documentation, merges similar prop- erties, and prioritizes them based on their criticality to system security. In particular, it merges overlapping properties that share operations or register types. Using the Common Vulnerabil- ity Scoring System (CVSS), it ranks security properties by their severity and assigns weights based on the role of the corresponding IP in the system (e.g., cryptographic cores and peripherals). Assert-O was trained and evaluated on OpenTitan, an open-source SoC design, where it processed documentation for six IPs, initially generating 183 security properties, which were optimized and reduced by 24.6% to 138 properties. The properties were ranked based on their severity, with the Reset Manager identified as the most security-critical module. SoCureLLM [134] is a hardware security verification framework that handles large-scale SoC designs. Its automated vulnerability detection method partitions the design into code snippets, generates additional context through summarization, and detects security policy violation. New security policies are created through threat model-based assessments. It detected 76.47% of security bugs across three vulnerable RISC-V SoCs, and develops 84 new security policies from additional designs. 4.4 Debugging Traditional hardware design debugging often involves meticulously reviewing lines of code, manu- ally identifying syntax errors, or logic flaws, which can be time-consuming and error-prone. LLMs, with their deep understanding of programming languages and hardware design principles, can analyze and interpret complex HDLs like Verilog or VHDL. They offer intelligent suggestions for code optimization, identify potential bug patterns, and even autonomously correct errors, thereby expediting the debugging cycle. RTLFixer [135] is a debugging framework that utilizes LLMs as autonomous language agents enhanced with RAG and ReAct. In particular, an LLM is designed for code generation. Modification functions are created by leveraging LLMs to analyze HDL manuals, expert notes, and user logs, extracting prevalent error patterns. An array of high-quality, industry-provided HDL codes serve as the basis for applying the generated modification functions, thereby producing a dataset of code pairs encompassing both faulty and corrected versions. HDL-Debugger achieves a pass-rate of up to 81.93% on an HDL dataset sourced from Huawei. Qayyum et al. [142] present a method that combines RAG with LLM for HDL bug identification and patching. They first split the specification file into smaller chunks and store them in a vector database. Then, HDL code is split into single lines, which are used to query the vector database for matching specification chunks. In case the LLM identifies a bug in the HDL code w.r.t. the given semantically retrieved specification, it creates a patch following the same HDL code pattern. Figure 9(a) illustrates the debugging framework of Qayyum et al. LiK [143] is an LLM-based solution for functional bug localization in Verilog. The model is fine-tuned on a bug location dataset, which is constructed by bug injection and reasoning thought reverse-engineering. LiK achieves a pass@1 localization accuracy of 93.3% on a test dataset based on RTLLM, surpassing GPT-4’s 77.9% and comparable to Claude-3.5’s 90.8%. The bug location obtained by LiK improves GPT-3.5’s bug repair efficiency (functional pass@1) from 40.39% to 58.92%. Wan et al. [144] construct the Chrysalis dataset by injecting logic bugs into HLS designs. Over 1,000 individual HLS programs are first collected from open-source projects. Then, common pre- silicon logic bugs are listed, including OOB access, infinite loop, and so on. Erroneous code are generated by injecting one or two types of bugs into the original design, which is done by prompting LLMs with context, requirement, and some instructing rules. SPICED+ [145] is an enhanced extension of the SPICED framework, specifically designed to not only detect and localize analog Trojans in A/MS (Analog/Mixed-Signal) circuits but also to mitigate them through iterative correction. While SPICED focuses on identifying Trojan-impacted nodes and detecting anomalies using LLMs guided by supervised learning rules and few-shot examples, SPICED+ introduces a confidence scoring metric and integrates multiple tools, including SPICED and HSPICE, to refine the detection process and ensure precise mitigation. SPICED+ iteratively removes suspect Trojan lines from SPICE netlists, reruns HSPICE simulations to validate circuit performance, and employs state management for rollback in case of adverse impacts. By incorporating confidence scores to prioritize suspect nodes and automating the correction workflow, SPICED+ achieves an average Trojan coverage of 93.3%, a Trojan mitigation rate (TMR) of 94.6%, and a false-positive rate of just 1.4%, significantly improving upon SPICED’s capabilities while maintaining zero area and power overheads. 5 Knowledge Representation and Retrieval LLMs for knowledge representation and retrieval are redefining how information is organized, accessed, and utilized in EDA. As hardware designs grow increasingly complex, the ability to effec- tively represent and retrieve knowledge from design specifications, technical documentation, and debugging logs has become critical. LLMs, particularly those fine-tuned for EDA-specific tasks, excel in extracting, structuring, and reasoning over vast amounts of unstructured and semi-structured data. They enable context-aware QA, assist in reviewing specifications, and identify patterns that aid in bug detection and analysis. By bridging the gap between natural language and technical design data, LLMs offer a transformative approach to streamlining EDA workflows, reducing man- ual effort, and enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of design and validation processes. Their ability to dynamically adapt to domain-specific knowledge makes them invaluable in addressing the growing information complexity in modern EDA systems. ACM Trans. Des. Autom. Electron. Built on a scalable, tool-based RAG architecture, ORAssistant leverages curated datasets from OpenROAD documentation, GitHub discussions, and other public resources to provide context-specific and reliable responses to user queries related to installation, command usage, flow setup, and debugging. By integrating hybrid retrieval techniques, including se- mantic and keyword-based searches, ORAssistant ensures accurate and context-aware answers with citations and hyperlinks. A novel dataset of 602 question-answer pairs was constructed to serve as the knowledge base, and the chatbot’s performance was evaluated using quantitative metrics (faithfulness, answer relevancy, context recall, and precision) and qualitative assessments by domain experts. While quantitative results showed no significant differences between models, qualitative feedback favored the ChatGPT- based chatbot (TEA/CGT) for its superior naturalness, coherence, and informativeness. Ask- EDA uses LLMs to generate natural language responses, RAG to enhance these responses with information retrieved from an external knowledge base using both dense and sparse retrieval meth- ods, and ADH to ensure accurate expansion of abbreviations by consulting a pre-built abbreviation dictionary. ChipAlign [159] presents a training-free approach to improve instruction alignment in domain- adapted LLMs for chip design. Current chip-specific LLMs, such as ChipNeMo, often lose general- purpose instruction-following capabilities during domain adaptation, limiting their usability in practical applications like QA and multi-turn interactions for hardware engineers. To address this, ChipAlign employs geodesic interpolation on a Riemannian manifold to merge the weights of a chip-specific LLM with a general instruction-aligned LLM, effectively combining chip expertise with strong instruction-following abilities. The method demonstrates superior performance across benchmarks, achieving a 26.6% improvement on the IFEval instruction-following benchmark and significant gains on chip-specific QA tasks, including 3.9% on OpenROAD QA and 8.25% on industrial chip QA. LADAC [166] leverages a domain-specified LLM to assist in the design of analog circuits. The methodology involves equipping the LLM with a local knowledge library rich in domain-specific insights and interactive tools that allow it to autonomously size transistors and obtain simulation outcomes. The LLM is trained to formulate optimized design strategies based on user specifications and foundational principles of analog circuit design. This approach integrates an LLM as a decision- making agent, which can iteratively refine the design through a combination of NLP and domain- specific knowledge. Authors showcased designing a two-stage amplifier, a 3-stage NMCNR amplifier, and a ring oscillator with LADAC. AmpAgent [167] is a multi-agent system based on LLMs for designing complex multi-stage amplifiers. AmpAgent consists of three agents: a Literature Analysis Agent, a Mathematics Reason- ing Agent, and a Device Sizing Agent. The Literature Analysis Agent retrieves key information from literature, the Mathematics Reasoning Agent decomposes the design problem by deriving key formulas, and the Device Sizing Agent, integrated with simulation interfaces and conventional optimization algorithms, sizes the multi-stage amplifier according to the divided sub-problems. This collaborative approach enables efficient and systematic design of multi-stage amplifiers, with each agent contributing to different aspects of the design process. AmpAgent has improved circuit performance by up to 27.25×, while reducing number of iterations and execution time. The LLANA framework [168] integrates LLMs with BO to enhance the generation of analog design-dependent parameter constraints. It leverages the few-shot learning abilities of LLMs to improve the efficiency of BO, enabling more effective exploration of the analog circuit design space. The LLMs are used to generate high-quality design points, while the BO process balances exploration and exploitation. The LLM is provided with natural language representations of BO components, allowing it to harness the unique advantages of LLMs, such as contextual understanding and rapid learning, to generate and refine analog layout constraints. ADO-LLM [169] also combines LLM with BO, leveraging the LLM’s ability to infuse domain knowledge to rapidly generate viable design points, addressing the inefficiency of BO in finding high-value design areas. The LLM is initialized with the circuit definition, design specifications, and design instructions, and it generates initial design points. These points are then evaluated using a circuit simulator, and the outcomes are used to further enrich the LLM’s training examples, creating a feedback loop that improves the quality of the shared dataset and the effectiveness of the BO process. The LLM is also guided through a series of steps, including interpreting the circuit definition, balancing tradeoffs in design specifications, and providing few-shot examples with diverse simulation results to enhance its design capabilities. PCBAgent addresses challenges unique to PCB placement, such as irregular boundaries, high component density, and rotation feasibility, by incorporating novel techniques like placement sequence optimization, mask-based legalization, and HPWL-guided action search. GPCB routing [173, 174] applies Generative Pre-Trained Transformers (GPTs) to automate and optimize PCB routing. The approach transforms PCB routing into a network-flow problem, tokenizing routing patterns and leveraging GPT models for learning and predicting routing strate- gies based on human expertise. Key innovations include a sliding window mechanism, a local memory with cross-attention, and a multi-information fusion method that integrates flow encoding, start/end points, and capacity information to enhance prediction accuracy. GPCB enables parallel routing, significantly improving routability, runtime, and wirelength optimization compared to state-of-the-art methods. Experimental results demonstrate 100% routability, reduced signal latency through optimized wirelength, and up to 6.67× faster runtime than existing solutions like FreeR- outing. By reimagining PCB routing as a token prediction task, GPCB showcases the potential of Transformer-based architectures for addressing complex, real-world routing challenges. Future directions include extending the method to bus routing, redistribution layers, and differential pair routing. Xiao et al. The frame- work, PrefixLLM, transforms prefix circuit synthesis into a structured text generation problem using a proprietary format called Structured Prefix Circuit Representation (SPCR). An iterative process is employed to generate valid SPCRs, ensuring correctness by integrating validation and feedback mechanisms. PrefixLLM also incorporates an iterative DSE framework to optimize prefix circuits for area and delay by utilizing a sorted circuit pool and custom prompts to guide the LLM in discovering high-quality designs. Experimental results demonstrate that PrefixLLM achieves up to a 3.70% area reduction compared to state-of-the-art methods and outperforms classical prefix circuits like Kogge-Stone and Brent-Kung under comparable delay constraints. He introduces that the near term will witness leveraging LLMs along three main vectors, namely design assistant to answer queries, prompt-based tool flows for live feedback, and graph generative models for incremental designs. He points out that these vectors can potentially revolutionize designer productivity, but perhaps not end quality of outcomes in physical design. 8 A 5-level Roadmap to LLM-empowered Autonomous EDA This survey has outlined the transformative potential of LLMs in the domain of EDA. We have explored how these powerful language models are evolving from basic assistants to increasingly sophisticated partners in the design process. To guide future research and development, we propose a 5-level roadmap that charts a path toward a future of intelligent and autonomous EDA: — L1 (Basic Application): This level represents the initial stage of LLM integration into EDA. LLMs act primarily as information retrieval and processing tools, assisting designers with tasks that do not directly involve the design process itself. They can search through vast libraries of documentation, answer questions about design principles and methodologies, summarize technical papers, and even provide natural language interfaces for existing EDA tools. This level is about making EDA knowledge and resources more accessible and user- friendly. Imagine asking an LLM to find the best documentation on a specific transistor model or to explain the concept of a certain design constraint in plain English. These are examples of the tasks that Level 1 LLMs excel at. Challenges. — Ensuring that the information retrieved or summarized by LLMs is accurate, relevant, and up-to-date is critical, since misinformation or outdated resources could mislead designers. — LLMs must be fine-tuned to handle the technical jargon, concepts, and structure of EDA data, which is often highly specialized and domain-specific. — Seamlessly integrating LLMs with existing EDA tools and workflows requires developing user-friendly interfaces and APIs. Opportunities. — LLMs can make complex EDA knowledge accessible to non-experts, fostering collaboration across interdisciplinary teams. — By handling tedious information retrieval, LLMs free designers to focus on creative and strategic tasks. — LLMs can be used as teaching aids, explaining complex design principles in plain language to students and new engineers. — L2 (Helpers): Level 2 moves beyond basic information retrieval and enters the realm of task automation. LLMs begin to actively assist designers by generating scripts for repetitive tasks, automating common design workflows, and even suggesting code completions. For example, an LLM can generate a script to set up a simulation based on a specific design requirement or suggest a missing line of code to fix a DRC error. This level focuses on making designers more efficient by eliminating tedious and time-consuming tasks. Think of it as having a programming assistant that can handle the repetitive grunt work while you focus on the more creative aspects of design. ACM Trans. Des. Autom. Electron. Syst., Vol. 30, No. 6, Article 90. Publication date: October 2025.

title: Large Language Models for EDA: Future or Mirage?
text: 90:40 Z. He et al. Challenges. — Automating workflows requires LLMs to handle edge cases and errors gracefully to avoid introducing bugs or disrupting the design process. — EDA workflows vary widely across tools, domains, and teams, creating a need for LLMs to adapt to different environments and requirements. — Automated workflows could inadvertently expose sensitive design data if not properly secured. Opportunities. — Automating repetitive tasks can significantly reduce development time and improve work- flow efficiency. — LLMs can help enforce best practices in script generation and workflows, leading to more consistent results across teams. — LLMs can learn from user feedback to provide increasingly tailored and effective automation solutions. — L3 (Active Design Participation): Level 3 is where LLMs become true partners in the de- sign process. They go beyond simple automation and begin to actively participate in de- sign decisions, offering suggestions, identifying design patterns, and even recommending components based on specific constraints. For example, an LLM could suggest a layout optimization based on an analysis of signal integrity or recommend a specific capacitor based on power consumption requirements. Level 3 LLMs can understand design context and constraints, providing valuable insights and guiding the design process toward more optimal solutions. Challenges. — LLMs must interpret design requirements, constraints, and tradeoffs across multiple do- mains, such as analog, digital, and mixed-signal design. — Achieving this level requires LLMs to process and generate insights from diverse data formats, including schematics, layouts, and performance metrics. — The complexity of modern designs demands an in-depth understanding of system-level interactions that is challenging for LLMs. Opportunities. — LLMs can assist designers in exploring alternative solutions, identifying tradeoffs, and optimizing for performance metrics. — By acting as a design partner, LLMs can enhance creativity, helping designers explore novel ideas they might not have considered. — LLMs can provide immediate feedback during the design process, reducing iteration cycles and improving the quality of final designs. — L4 (Guided Optimization and Decision Making): At Level 4, LLMs transition from collaborators to autonomous agents. They can now perform complex design tasks with minimal human intervention, exploring vast design spaces, making tradeoffs based on predefined constraints, and continuously adapting to evolving requirements. Imagine an LLM that can explore a vast range of circuit topologies, optimize for performance and power consumption, and present the best-performing design based on predefined criteria. This level represents a significant leap towards truly intelligent and automated EDA. Challenges. — Developing advanced optimization techniques that can balance tradeoffs across multiple conflicting objectives (e.g., power, performance, area) is a major hurdle. ACM Trans. Des. Autom. Electron. Syst., Vol. 30, No. 6, Article 90. Publication date: October 2025.

title: Large Language Models for EDA: Future or Mirage?
text: Large Language Models for EDA: Future or Mirage? 90:41 — Handling large-scale design spaces and high-dimensional optimization problems requires significant computational resources and efficient algorithms. — Ensuring the correctness of LLM-generated designs is critical, as errors at this stage could have catastrophic downstream consequences. Opportunities. — LLMs can explore a much larger range of design possibilities than humans, potentially uncovering innovative solutions. — By taking over time-intensive optimization tasks, LLMs can dramatically accelerate the design cycle. — LLMs with real-time feedback loops can learn from past results to continuously refine their optimization strategies. — L5 (Autonomous Agent and Super-Human Performance): Level 5 represents the ultimate goal of LLM integration into EDA. LLMs at this level become autonomous design agents, potentially surpassing human capabilities. They can perform tasks such as generative de- sign, synthesizing new circuits and systems, and even iterating and optimizing designs in a completely unsupervised manner. This level is about pushing the boundaries of design innovation, exploring uncharted design spaces, and potentially leading to breakthroughs that were previously unimaginable. Imagine an LLM that can invent new circuit architectures, optimize for performance beyond human intuition, and even learn and adapt to new design challenges without human guidance. Challenges. — Ensuring that autonomous LLMs consistently produce reliable and safe designs is para- mount, especially when operating without human supervision. — Autonomous agents raise ethical questions about accountability, intellectual property ownership, and the potential misuse of these systems. — Achieving this level requires unprecedented computational power and access to massive, high-quality datasets. Opportunities. — Autonomous LLMs can explore uncharted design spaces, leading to revolutionary advance- ments in circuit architectures and EDA methodologies. — Fully autonomous systems can operate continuously, dramatically reducing time-to-market for new designs. — LLMs at this level could innovate by integrating knowledge and methodologies from other domains, such as biology or quantum computing, into EDA. Figure 12 illustrates the proposed 5-level roadmap (including Level 0 meaning no LLM). This 5-level roadmap provides a structured approach to the integration and advancement of LLMs in EDA. As we move from basic applications to fully autonomous agents, each level builds upon the previous one, increasing the complexity and depth of integration, representing a significant advancement in the role and capabilities of LLMs in EDA. By leveraging the power of these sophisticated language models, we can accelerate innovation, improve design efficiency, and unlock new frontiers in electronic design. The future of EDA lies in embracing the collaborative potential of LLMs, where human ingenuity and AI capabilities work together to push the boundaries of what’s possible. 9 Discussions Despite their transformative potential, applying LLMs to EDA faces several key challenges that must be addressed to ensure their effective and ethical deployment. Below, we discuss these issues in detail and outline potential solutions. Data Privacy. EDA workflows often involve proprietary information, including sensitive circuit designs, intellectual property (IP), and fabrication details. Leveraging LLMs typically requires large datasets, which may expose private or confidential data during model training or inference. Training LLMs on sensitive data without strong privacy guarantees risks disclosing proprietary IPs, violating non-disclosure agreements (NDAs), and exposing trade secrets. Besides, many commercial LLMs (e.g., GPT models) rely on cloud-based APIs, which may lead to concerns about data leakage during inference. In particular, Extraction attacks [195] typically refer to attempts by adversaries to extract sensitive information or insights from ML models or their associated data. It has been shown that LLMs memorize and leak training data [196], even without a surrogate dataset [197]. Defense methods either improve training, such as corpora de-identification [198] and safety alignment [21], or are deployed during inference, such as malicious detection [199]. Reliability. Model reliability refers to the ability of an LLM to consistently produce accurate, trust- worthy, and predictable outputs. Unreliable behavior, such as generating incorrect, incomplete, or nonsensical results, can have significant consequences, including design failures, wasted resources, or even security vulnerabilities. LLMs often exhibit issues such as hallucinations [200], where the model generates fabricated or inaccurate outputs, and inconsistencies [201], where it provides different answers to similar queries. Such behavior can lead to a lack of trust in the model’s outputs, particularly in mission-critical applications. Additionally, the black-box nature of LLMs makes it difficult to interpret their decisions or trace the source of errors, further compounding reliability concerns. Self-reflection [202] has been proposed to tackle the hallucination challenge through this feedback process. Retrieval Augmentation also reduces hallucination in knowledge-grounded conversations [203]. CoT [25] is a series of intermediate reasoning steps that significantly improves the ability of LLMs to perform complex reasoning. LLM uncertainty estimation [204] has also been greatly explored. Workforce. The adoption of LLMs in EDA may disrupt traditional workflows, raising concerns about the potential impact on the workforce. The integration of LLMs into industry operations ACM Trans. title: Large Language Models for EDA: Future or Mirage?
text: Large Language Models for EDA: Future or Mirage? 90:43 offers numerous benefits [205], such as automation of repetitive tasks, improving data driven decision-making, driving cost reductions and improving operational efficiency, and enhancing the customer experience through highly personalized interactions. However, LLMs also face ethical and societal challenges, including potential job displacement and the risk of misinformation, as they can be used to generate misleading content at scale. A recent research [206] shows that over 46% of jobs in software development could have over half their tasks affected by LLMs with simple interfaces and general training. From a technical perspective, it is demonstrated that explainable AI improves human-AI collaboration, allowing domain experts to validate AI predictions against their own domain knowledge [207]. Dataset Quality. The quality and diversity of training datasets directly impact the performance and generalizability of LLMs in EDA tasks. However, sourcing comprehensive datasets for EDA remains a significant challenge. EDA datasets, especially for AMS circuits, are scarce due to proprietary restrictions and limited open-source contributions. LLMs trained on unbalanced datasets may exhibit biases, leading to suboptimal performance for niche applications or novel designs. As for LLM pretraining, it is predicted in [208] that models will be trained on datasets roughly equal in size to the available stock of public human text data between 2026 and 2032. Generating high-quality synthetic data may pave the way for developing next-gen LLMs [209]. It may worth exploring using synthetic data generation techniques (e.g., procedural generation of SPICE netlists or Verilog code) to create diverse and scalable datasets. Data augmentation [210] is a pivotal technique for enhancing model performance by diversifying training examples without the need for additional data collection. Self-instruct [211] represents a bootstrapping method for inducing instruction following capabilities with minimal human-labeled data, which might be extended to dataset generation. 10 Conclusion In this comprehensive survey, we have systematically reviewed the application of LLMs in the domain of EDA, categorizing the existing literature into four primary areas: code generation, verification and debugging, knowledge representation, and optimization/modeling. Our analysis has highlighted the significant potential of LLMs to revolutionize various aspects of the EDA process, from design synthesis and optimization to verification and documentation. Through code generation, LLMs automate the creation of HDLs, system-level designs, and flow scripts, significantly accelerating prototyping and reducing manual effort. In verification and debugging, they enhance design correctness by automating testbench generation, assertion synthesis, fault localization, and error correction, streamlining the process of detecting and resolving functional and security issues. Knowledge representation leverages the reasoning capabilities of LLMs to encode and retrieve design knowledge, aiding in specification understanding, bug classification, and efficient decision-making through QA systems. Finally, in optimization/modeling, LLMs enable improvements in design metrics such as PPA by automating circuit sizing, layout refinement, and workflow optimization. Together, these capabilities highlight the potential of LLMs to enhance productivity, improve design quality, and drive innovation in EDA, offering a new paradigm for tackling complex design and engineering challenges. However, realizing their full potential requires addressing key challenges, including data privacy, model reliability, dataset quality, and workforce adaptation, ensuring their deployment is both effective and ethical. We have proposed a 5-level roadmap to guide the progressive integration and advancement of LLMs in EDA. By following the 5-level roadmap and addressing the associated challenges, we can unlock new levels of productivity, innovation, and efficiency in the EDA domain. As the technology continues to evolve, the potential for LLMs to transform the field of EDA is immense, and we look forward to the exciting developments and breakthroughs that lie ahead. ACM Trans. Des. Autom. Electron. Syst., Vol. 30, No. 6, Article 90. Publication date: October 2025.
